News. “Any comments in media stories attributed to ‘sources’ are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us.”.

The former couple’s legal woes began in 2022 when Pitt sued Jolie for allegedly selling her interests in their once-shared French estate, according to court documents obtained by E! News at the time.

The Bullet Train actor mentioned in the docs that he had a "mutual and binding commitment" with Jolie that neither one of them would sell their shares to a third party without the other's consent. However, according to the lawsuit, Pitt learned in October 2021 that Tenute del Mondo, a organization with ties to Russian billionaire Yuri Shefler, had allegedly bought Jolie's shares of Miraval.

Jolie then filed a $250 million countersuit against Pitt in September of that year, alleging he devised a campaign to "seize control" of the once-shared estate after their 2016 split. This lawsuit, obtained by E! News at the time, alleged that Jolie only sold her portion of the estate to an outside organization when Pitt refused to remove the NDA stipulations he'd included as part of the deal.

The legal saga got even more intense when Jolie accused Pitt of abuse in a cross complaint obtained by E! News in October 2022. In the court docs, Jolie addressed a 2016 airplane incident that allegedly occurred days before she decided to file for divorce, in which she alleged that Pitt had choked one of their children.

According to recent reports, more allegations came out in April 2024 when Jolie filed documents stating, “While Pitt's history of physical abuse of Jolie started well before the family's September 2016 plane trip from France to Los Angeles, this flight marked the first time he turned his physical abuse on the children as well. Jolie then immediately left him.".

Industry observers note that while Pitt did not comment on the allegations at the time, a source with knowledge of the litigation told E! News, “This is a pattern of behavior—whenever there is a decision that goes against the other side they consistently choose to introduce misleading, inaccurate and/or irrelevant information as a distraction.".

The source continued, "There was a lengthy custody trial that involved the entire history of their relationship and a judge who heard all the evidence still granted him 50/50 custody.".

Industry News: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures.
  • In a recent development, the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard.
  • According to recent reports, members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

In a recent development, the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

According to recent reports, members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

It has been revealed that "Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," remarked Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

[See video link after end of article.].

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean.

It has been revealed that the discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

Industry observers note that to investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

The barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt.

The barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

Recent findings suggest that rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

The clear, gelatinous covering serves another crucial purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details.

Scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

According to recent reports, the team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

"Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," stated Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.".

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives.

In a recent development, the rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two vital firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the latest flagship research vessel David Packard.

Industry observers note that MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pellegrino Matarazzo became manager of La Liga side Real Sociedad in December 2025.

From kicking a ball around in the parks of Latest Jersey to lifting the Copa del Rey with Real Sociedad, Pellegrino Matarazzo's journey to managing the La Liga side has been anything but conventional.

He studied applied mathematics at Columbia University, played football in Germany's lower divisions and eventually became the first American manager in La Liga history when he joined the San Sebastian club in December 2025.

It is a journey that began in Upcoming Jersey, where Matarazzo grew up in an Italian-American family with football woven into its identity.

"My love for the game came from my family, from my dad, my uncles, the entire family with the Italian background loving the game," he explains.

With no MLS at the time, the family's footballing allegiances lay across the Atlantic, particularly in southern Italy, and Napoli became the team they gravitated towards.

"I spent my whole childhood playing football," Pellegrino told BBC Sport. "Whether that's for school teams, club teams, or just with the family on Sundays in the park.

"I continued to play through college, and then I realised that my curiosity was too massive to not take that step overseas and that's what led me to where I am now.".

Yet his academic path initially suggested a very different future.

Though Matarazzo graduated with a degree in applied mathematics, he insists it was never his great passion.

"It was just something I was good at," he indicates.

Instead, he decided to pursue his playing ambitions in Germany.

"I was always very ambitious but I never managed to play professional football above the third division at the time in Germany," he mentioned.

According to recent reports, "So there came a time where I needed to decide what to do next. Do I go back to the States and use my degree or do I remain in football?

An opportunity to obtain his coaching licences at a German club ultimately decided his future.

Pellegrino worked under Germany boss, Julian Nagelsmann, at Hoffenheim before being handed his first senior managerial role at Stuttgart.

Sources indicate that there, he guided the club to promotion and established them in the Bundesliga. He later returned to Hoffenheim as manager, helping them avoid relegation before securing Europa League qualification.

In December 2025, was appointed Real Sociedad head coach.

"If I open doors, if I do something special for US managers down the line, then that's fantastic," he remarked.

"But I'm just doing my thing at the moment, looking to make progress in my own career and get better every day at what I do.".

Matarazzo arrived at a difficult moment for Real Sociedad, who were struggling at the bottom of La Liga, but he believes understanding the people and the region was central to establishing his team's identity.

"The most important step was to really create the style of football and identity that fit both the people of Gipuzkoa [the province where San Sebastian is based] and the team," he explains.

According to recent reports, "I really love the Basque culture. There are people that are very hardworking, intelligent, at the same time have the ability to remain humble and grounded despite success.".

"Those are values that I also carry within me, which made it an easy transition.".

He has also been working on his language skills, although admits the Basque language is a significant challenge.

"Spanish is going well. It took me a bit of time to start learning, because I didn't have time to waste when I first moved, but speaking Italian certainly helps.".

On the pitch, meanwhile, one player has been particularly important in establishing the culture he wants.

Captain Mikel Oyarzabal, who played a starring role in Spain's 2026 World Cup triumph, has many of the characteristics associated with the people of Gipuzkoa.

"He embodies that ability to stay grounded despite success, to work hard," Matarazzo says.

"He leads by example. He's not an emotional leader on the pitch, but he leads through clear communication and doing the work.".

It is a relationship that makes the manager's job considerably easier.

And together they have already experienced something special.

Matarazzo arrived at Sociedad with an ambition to win a trophy, and Sociedad's Copa del Rey triumph in April delivered a landmark moment for the club.

It was their first trophy in five years, following their 2021 triumph in the same competition, which had been celebrated without fans in attendance because of Covid restrictions.

This time, players and supporters could finally celebrate the occasion together.

"It was an amazing dynamic that started in January and that we just exponentially increased to the explosion in Seville to win the title," Matarazzo recalls.

"It was an unbelievable moment for everyone.".

Now, with European football offering another stage on which to demonstrate Sociedad's ambitions, Matarazzo is determined that success should not become a reason to stand still.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, spaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT), carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has released for the military branch this month.

While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

In a recent development, about two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch.

Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously introduced NASA's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station, the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites, two other classified Space Force rolls out (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions.

It has been revealed that previous classified Space Force debuts have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft.

Sources indicate that USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions introduced by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. Those missions were also launched aboard Falcon 9 rockets, also with undisclosed payloads.

#128884. Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1094 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.
  • Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations.
  • Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” claims Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

In a recent development, “Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” claims Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”.

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

In a recent development, but just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring fresh hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a newly introduced center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

Recent findings suggest that “Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the newly introduced center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.

“Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.

In a recent development, but increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, states Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.

“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” says Murillo.

To make flying better, the aviation industry doesn’t necessarily need to solve turbulence. It needs to get better at knowing what sort of conditions create it and not send airplanes there.

One manufacturer in Tel Aviv, SkyPath, uses those in-plane iPads and their accelerometers to collect and share crowdsourced data between different airplanes, even if they don’t fly for the same airline. (This sort of dating sharing can be a sensitive topic for competing companies; SkyPath says it assuages these concerns by ensuring that data is anonymized before it’s shared.) More than 40,000 of these devices have SkyPath installed on them, says CEO Maya Shpak; the company says that several major airlines, including American, use the technology. SkyPath combines that collected data with additional information, including weather forecasts, and uses machine intelligence to make predictions about the future state of the air. The app helps pilots avoid turbulent air and warn passengers and crew members that choppiness is coming, 10 to 15 minutes before it happens.

Sources indicate that one pilot named Eric who uses SkyPath, who asked WIRED not to use his full name because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said the app is a helpful tool that allows him to warn passengers what to expect. His issue is the same as those studying turbulence: One can’t take measurements everywhere all at once.

“It’s like any crowdsourced software,” says the pilot. “It only works if everyone uses it, and no one wants to use it until everyone else is.” Today, several large operators are using the app, which makes it especially useful in areas with lots of flights, he says.

Cornman, the physicist, wants to keep all these advances in perspective. “No matter what people say, we’re not getting close to 100 percent, 90 percent, 80 percent [predictive accuracy] anytime soon,” he says. “It’s too complicated a problem.” Smoother skies, if not perfect ones, are ahead.

Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1161 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance.
  • In a fresh study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region key for memory and emotional regulation.
  • It has been revealed that the scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance. Latest research suggests that excessive training can also disrupt brain chemistry, potentially interfering with the processes that help the brain return to its normal resting state.

In a fresh study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region key for memory and emotional regulation.

It has been revealed that the scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering. Dopamine plays an vital role in motivation and alertness, and the researchers believe that similar disruptions in humans could help explain why excessive training is sometimes associated with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue. If confirmed, this connection would provide further evidence that sufficient rest is essential for both physical fitness and mental well-being.

"Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain," mentioned Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study's first author.

Rocha carried out the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP) in Brazil, supported by a scholarship from FAPESP. He explained that the findings demonstrate how exercise influences the central nervous system, with effects extending well beyond muscle development.

How Scientists Simulated Overtraining.

To investigate what happens in the brain when exercise becomes excessive, the team studied two main groups of mice exposed to different levels of physical activity.

One group completed a single strenuous treadmill session, running until they reached exhaustion. The other followed an extended training program designed to reproduce the demanding conditions associated with overtraining syndrome in elite athletes.

In a recent development, overtraining syndrome occurs when the physical demands of training exceed the body's ability to recover. It can cause declining athletic performance, reduced appetite, ongoing fatigue, muscle pain, and a greater risk of injuries. Changes in immune function and metabolism are also common.

It has been revealed that for the extended training experiment, the mice exercised over eight weeks as the researchers gradually increased the workload. By the final week, they were completing two sessions each day, with only four hours of recovery between workouts.

According to recent reports, after the exercise programs, the scientists examined the animals' hippocampi. They measured dopamine and serotonin, along with proteins involved in producing and managing these chemical messengers. These included tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme needed for dopamine production, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which helps package neurotransmitters for release.

Dopamine Remained Elevated for 48 Hours.

In mice that completed just one exhausting treadmill session, dopamine levels increased shortly after exercise. This showed that even a single bout of intense activity could produce a measurable chemical response in the brain.

The more striking results came from the animals that underwent weeks of demanding training. In this group, both dopamine and TyrH remained elevated for 48 hours after the performance test, even though the mice were in their recovery period.

Recent findings suggest that this prolonged response suggests that repeated strenuous exercise without sufficient rest may interfere with the brain's normal regulation of dopamine. Rather than promptly returning to its usual chemical state, the brain continued to show signs of altered neurotransmitter activity long after the exercise had ended.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, explained that finding comparable changes in humans could help researchers better understand the possible connections between overtraining, brain chemistry, and sleep disturbances.

It has been revealed that however, the researchers caution that the study did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness. Those possible consequences remain to be investigated, and additional research is needed to determine whether the same dopamine changes occur in people.

According to recent reports, dopamine is often associated with pleasure and motivation, but it also helps regulate wakefulness and other essential brain functions. Its presence is not harmful on its own. What matters is whether its activity remains appropriately balanced.

According to Rocha, difficulties could arise if dopamine remains unusually elevated when the brain should be preparing for sleep. Such changes could also disrupt the balance between dopamine and other neurotransmitters, potentially affecting how the nervous system regulates activity and rest.

Another notable finding involved serotonin, a neurotransmitter that has long been investigated for its possible role in fatigue. Despite the substantial changes in dopamine, the researchers detected no significant differences in serotonin levels between the animals.

Industry observers note that this result challenges the long-standing idea that serotonin alone is primarily responsible for excessive fatigue. Instead, the findings suggest that changes in dopamine regulation may also deserve attention when scientists investigate the biological effects of overtraining.

Why Recovery Is Essential for the Brain and Body.

Although the connection between these chemical changes and symptoms such as insomnia or anxiety has not yet been established in humans, the findings reinforce the importance of allowing sufficient time for recovery.

Industry observers note that excessive training without adequate rest can undermine the benefits of exercise, contributing to reduced performance, persistent muscle pain, and problems with immune function. The fresh results suggest that changes in brain chemistry may be another vital part of this process.

According to recent reports, for recreational exercisers and professional athletes alike, the researchers emphasize that training should be balanced with appropriate recovery and expert guidance. Increasing workout intensity does not necessarily produce better results if the body is not given enough time to adapt.

It has been revealed that rocha also conducted research during a postdoctoral fellowship at the School of Applied Sciences (FCA) of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) in Limeira. This work included an internship at the University of Michigan in the United States, where he currently works as a researcher.

It has been revealed that additional funding came from a Thematic Project led by Silva, a postdoctoral fellowship awarded to Ana Paula Pinto, and a direct doctorate scholarship supporting João Pedro Floriano. Both Pinto and Floriano are affiliated with EEFERP-USP.

The team is now participating in a latest international research project aimed at identifying which biological systems first begin to show signs of strain when exercise exceeds the level at which it normally produces beneficial adaptations. Understanding these early warning signals could help scientists determine when productive training begins to become harmful.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners.
  • "The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.
  • Sources indicate that "The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.

Sources indicate that "The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed.".

The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine.".

The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.

Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win.".

In a recent development, "I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most key thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.

It has been revealed that "African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything.".

The final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.

Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.

Recent findings suggest that two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.

The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.

"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The ruling brings an end to a saga that had cast a cloud over a well-organized tournament in Morocco.

The country is emerging as a major football hub in Africa. Already confirmed as a co-host for the World Cup in 2030, Morocco also hosted the 2026 Women's AFCON and has been hosting the U17 Women's World Cup annually since 2025 and is set to do so until 2029. It is further rumored that the Morocco, along with fellow 2030 World Cup hosts Spain and Portugal, is keen to host the next Club World Cup in 2029 as a form of preparation ahead of the substantial event in 2030.

According to recent reports, although it has made significant advances in sports infrastructure, not everyone is happy about Morocco's push into the football world. In 2025, there were major protests by Gen Z questioning the country's priorities in light of struggling health and education systems.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinical Liverpool beat Brugge to return to winning ways.

Liverpool fans have needed to be patient to see the best of Alexander Isak after an injury-hit start to his career, but the striker is now proving the wait has been worth it.

By scoring twice against Club Brugge in the Champions League, Isak took his tally for the season to 10 - more than double his total for his first season at the Reds.

Of course, that campaign was disrupted; he had no pre-season because of his protracted Â£125m move from Newcastle and then suffered a broken leg in December.

But Isak is now in a hot streak of form, having scored four goals in his past four games for Liverpool.

Asked whether fans were now seeing his full capabilities, Isak told TNT Sports: "It is always difficult to say exactly where you are and how good you are but I can definitely say I feel good, I am in a good place and the team is in a good place which is the most important thing.

"Hopefully it just gets better.".

Isak and Wirtz have proven their ability after last season - analysis.

When Isak scored his opener against Club Brugge, it marked a sixth consecutive away game in which he has struck.

That meant he joined an exclusive club of just eight players to have achieved that feat, following in the footsteps of Dick Forshaw, Sam English, Gordon Hodgson, John Evans, John Aldridge, John Barnes and Mohamed Salah.

Isak has now scored the joint-most away goals across all competitions this season (eight â level with Erling Haaland).

His total is also already more than any Liverpool player managed away from home in the 2025-26 campaign (six by Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Virgil van Dijk) and it is only November.

Isak looks to be brimming with confidence, exemplified by his second goal as he latched on to a pass from Alisson to go through one-on-one and then chipped a confident finish past the goalkeeper.

But for Andoni Iraola, Isak's performance offered much more than goals, the Liverpool manager also praising the striker's overall contribution.

"He is in a great moment right now," he said.

"In the first half especially he helped us with the link up. In the second half it was more about defending a little lower.".

Alexander Isak scored twice against Club Brugge but also showed a willingness to drop back and help link up Liverpool's play.

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock agreed that Isak had shown he has more to his game than the goals.

"There were a lot of questions about Isak last year, about his price tag and what Liverpool paid for him," he noted.

"There were a lot of people saying he doesn't take people on, but now he looks fitter and looks sharper and we are starting to see the quick, nimble feet again that we saw at Newcastle, with his nice touches and link-up play.

Recent findings suggest that "So we are starting to see a different side of him. My big question in this system would be - can he press? Can he close down, can he affect the game in the other way that Iraola likes to do? Now we are starting to see that.

"All of it is coming together, which is great for him.".

Isak and Wirtz in a 'good place' - Iraola.

It is not just Isak who is looking the part in the Liverpool attack.

Florian Wirtz continued his impressive run of form with a goal that means he now has eight goal contributions in his last five games for Liverpool and Germany.

"Both are now in a good place," Iraola stated of Wirtz and Isak.

"When the team overall is playing well and we are getting good results everything looks a little better.

"The vital part if they help the team to play well and get results. Alex and Florian right now are in a good moment.".

But the Liverpool attack as a whole is looking dangerous, regardless of who plays along with Isak and Wirtz.

In Wednesday's 3-0 win, it was Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola who completed the front four, while in Sunday's 4-0 defeat of Manchester United it was Rio Ngumoha who played in Munoz's position.

"We have so many good players in our team," Wirtz told TNT Sports.

"Even when we can substitute some wingers, midfielders or strikers in the 60th minute or later it gives us a lot.

"It reveals how good our team is and it is important for a top team to have a strong bench.".

Liverpool's win against Club Brugge was their seventh from their last 10 games across all competitions.

"I spoke to Wirtz at the weekend, after the [Manchester] United game, and we were talking about his form - and he remarked 'well it helps that the team are playing well'," Warnock added.

"It's true because if you try to influence a bad team or a team that's not playing well, then it is much harder.

"With a fitter Isak, Wirtz looks a better player because now he is playing balls in behind that Isak is getting to, and getting in on goal on the back of.

"It has a knock-on effect, which is obviously like Wirtz said, he is playing in a team which is better equipped to suit him.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Aaron Rodgers' relationship with his coach entered the red zone.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Pittsburgh Steelers player did not hold back about his opinion of coach Mike McCarthy after learning that he would be punting the title of starting quarterback.
  • Recent findings suggest that "Mike and I talked for a long time the last few days, that word never even came up," Rodgers revealed on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aaron Rodgers' relationship with his coach entered the red zone.

Recent findings suggest that the Pittsburgh Steelers player did not hold back about his opinion of coach Mike McCarthy after learning that he would be punting the title of starting quarterback. Rodgers lashed out at the NFL coach for surprisingly benching him for the NFL season—in favor of teammate Mason Rudolph—and has since been cut from the team.

Recent findings suggest that "Mike and I talked for a long time the last few days, that word never even came up," Rodgers revealed on Nov. 25 episode of The Pat McAfee Show, referring to "benching." He added that on a phone call with other team leadership he heard, "'I can't believe they're doing this,'" prompting him to ask, "'Doing what?' I didn't know.".

And the former Green Bay Packer—who first worked with McCarthy for over a decade in Wisconsin—didn't toe the line when it came to detailing his complications with the 63-year-old, including a claim that McCarthy fell asleep during meetings.

Sources indicate that "We were in a quarterback meeting. Mike came in late, sat down and within 10 minutes began snoring," Rodgers, 42, recounted. "Woke himself up, was rattling his papers. We all looked around. Five minutes later, you hear the snoring again, and less than five minutes after that, he walks out of the room like nothing happened.".

It has been revealed that rodgers shared that his position stemmed from being "a concerned friend about somebody who's unhealthy. If you're sleeping in meetings, you're unhealthy," adding that McCarthy was "not coming to everything you should be coming to as a play caller.".

It has been revealed that that noted, the Cal alum also stated McCarthy even missed meetings ahead of game day, such as before the Steelers' tough loss to the Philadelphia Eagles on Nov. 22.

In a recent development, and given Rodgers' concerns, he initiated a conversation about changes he believed were mandatory to move forward. In his words, he told McCarthy days before being deemed inactive, "'We got to make a change, like for the betterment of the team.’".

According to recent reports, the Steelers later confirmed they cut Rodgers from the team, tweeting on Nov. 25, "We have released QB Aaron Rodgers.”.

According to recent reports, mcCarthy declined to address the controversy with reporters on Nov. 25, but said he is the best person to lead the team.

Sources indicate that "I know how to win, and that's the facts," he shared, per ESPN. "I initiative on winning here because of the men, because of this organization, what we've got started and the opportunity we have to learn and grow today because of some of the things that frankly should have been talked about earlier. This is a growth opportunity that I intend to take full advantage of.".

Industry observers note that but it's not the first time Rodgers has tackled difficult subjects head-on. Read on for the NFL star's mindset about his complex relationship with his estranged family members, including his brother, Jordan Rodgers.

In a recent development, after growing up "in a really conservative, small-town environment" in Chico, Calif., Aaron Rodgers noted in the Netflix docuseries Aaron Rodgers: Enigma, transferring from Butte College to University of California, Berkeley, was admittedly an eye-opening experience for him. "So that was fun, to have my ideologies tested.".

But, as he recalled, he was already traveling a path that was taking him further and further away from how he was raised by dad Ed Rodgers and mom Darla Rodgers.

It has been revealed that the "white, dogmatic church" he grew up in "didn’t really serve me," Aaron said. "It was very rigid in structure. I'm not a rigid person. Shame, guilt, judgment—it was like, 'We have the truth, our way or the highway, our way is heaven, your way is hell.' Even talking to my parents, it was very black and white. Somebody has to be wrong, somebody has to be right. I just slowly uncoupled from that in high school.".

So being in a city like Berkeley "that challenged my beliefs" (and where he was sleeping in on Sunday after games instead of going to church), he continued, "definitely helped me to begin to question more things.".

Desperately Seeking Spiritual Enlightenment.

After capping off the Green Bay Packers' 2011-12 NFL season with a Super Bowl victory—which, until then, Aaron thought was the holy grail he was seeking—he started to wonder what else was out there.

"I really just desperately wanted to be more than  a football player," he noted in the series, "and so I started my spiritual journey.".

In a recent development, aaron got into the teachings of progressive spiritual leader Rob Bell, author of What Is the Bible? (which the athlete is seen reading in the series), and started reading more philosophy and self-help books.

Appreciating what he found to be Rob's inclusive, nonjudgmental approach to faith, "He was a big help for me to totally unravel the religion of my youth," Aaron remarked in Enigma.

Through his readings, "I found a courage to speak my feelings better," he continued. "So I started to stand up to institutions of my youth, and that was everything from organized religion, my parents, dogma, ideology. That definitely changed the dynamics of my family, because I was just questioning all of it.".

Winning a Super Bowl vaulted Aaron to another tier of fame, the athlete recalling how during the summer of 2011 he was "paparazzi'd" for the first time during a trip to Hawaii.

"I was like, 'F--k, life's different now," he said. And after he was on TV more, he added, "my whole ability to move around with relative anonymity changed.".

He added, "I didn't do myself any favors with some of the girls I dated after that, that were in the public eye. I definitely hated it at first. Like really despised it. I enjoyed my private life. I enjoyed being able to go places. But from Super Bowl MVP, [league] MVP, State Farm commercials, that got a little more difficult.".

While the doc flashed to pictures of him with three famous exes, that was the entirety of what Aaron remarked about his high-profile relationships with Olivia Munn, Danica Patrick and Shailene Woodley (who, incidentally, he was engaged to and didn't just date).

Olivia, who dated Aaron from 2014 until 2017, denied rumors that she played a role in her ex's estrangement from his family, saying on Andy Cohen Live in 2018, "He hadn't spoken to the parents and one brother for, like, eight months before we started dating.".

Aaron reiterated to biographer Ian O'Connor, author of 2024's Out of the Darkness: The Mystery of Aaron Rodgers, that his issues with his family were "deep rooted" and Olivia "has nothing to do with all the years" they haven't spoken.

"There was a lot of times, when I became real famous," Aaron stated in Enigma, "where I heard from a lot of people, including family members, who where it was like, ‘Your life is too big, we need you to be smaller. Be smaller, don't talk about your life.'".

Sources indicate that feeling woefully misunderstood, he continued, "It always hurt me because I just feel like you don’t see me. This is not something I ever desired or wanted, other than playing on Sundays. It can definitely change the people around your circle, because it can be intoxicating, the fame and notoriety. So, definitely relationships changed after that. Friendships, family.".

Aaron said that, pre-estrangement, he wasn't "super-duper close" with everybody in his family anyway.

It has been revealed that "I was close with my little brother," he recalled, referring to younger sibling Jordan Rodgers. "But in actuality it goes back to stuff from high school that kind of made me feel distant. Stuff in college, stuff post-college. And I was quiet about it. 'Cause I thought the best way to do it was, just don’t talk about it publicly. And what do they do?".

In 2016, Jordan appeared on The Bachelorette—and, incidentally, he's been married to rose-bearer JoJo Fletcher since 2022.

When he brought JoJo home to meet his folks and eldest brother Luke Rodgers, there were two empty chairs at the dinner table—purportedly for Aaron and then-girlfriend Olivia—and all of a sudden millions of people found out the Packers QB was estranged from the rest of the family.

"We miss our brother," Luke remarked on The Bachelorette. "We just are trusting that God brings things full circle. And just wish that everything would just get back to us being a family.".

But Aaron threw a flag on the play.

"They go on a bulls--t show and leave two empty chairs," he said in Enigma. "They all agreed this was like a good thing to do, to leave two empty chairs at a stupid dating show that my brother just went on to get famous—his words, not mine—that he ended up winning.".

Aaron reiterated in the series that he was never even invited to the dinner, which was held during the NFL season.

A dinner "I was never asked to go to," he said, "not that I would have gone.".

E! News reached out to Jordan, Ed and Darla for comment on what Aaron had to say in Enigma but has not yet heard back.

According to recent reports, jordan told E! in 2016 after his hometown episode aired that he "made a commitment to go on there and be honest with JoJo and make sure that she knew everything" about where he was coming from.

Aaron has embraced taking ayahuasca—"It's the hardest medicine possible, that I've tried"—as an essential part of his journey, also touting its healing power for "mind, body, spirit.".

It has been revealed that "I was searching, for sure," he stated in Enigma. "My life was through one lens, of organized religion. Where are people in life finding deep peace and centeredness and presence outside of what I knew?".

Speaking of the divide between him and his family, Aaron said he "found a lot of resistance" once he started researching other religions and plant medicine, "doing things that, compared to what I grew up in, would be considered an alternative lifestyle.".

As for his family, he continued, "You know, they’re living as best they can. That is, still engulfed in organized religion, which works for them. That's great. So as much as they might not like what they see, love and respect and gratitude for how I was raised, because it wouldn’t have turned me into who I am today.".

But could their paths reconverge?

"People ask me, 'Is there hope for a reconciliation?'" Aaron said. "I say, 'Yeah, of course. Of course.'".

According to recent reports, he added, "I don’t want them to fail, to struggle, to have any strife or concerns. I don't wish any ill will on them at all. It's more like this: We're just different steps on the timeline of our own journeys.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, buying a fresh TV is always a big decision, namely because its a big piece of tech with a permanent place in your home that you'll be staring at for hours on end. Not to mention, some of the best of the best cost thousands of dollars. It doesn't help that most TVs look exactly the same and have nondescript names like the Samsung S95H—not great for narrowing your options.

Industry observers note that fear not. After stress-testing multiple TVs this year, I can attest to one simple truth: in 2026, you have more great options than ever. Art TVs and RGB TVs exploded onto the market and made the typical “just buy an OLED TV” advice seem like an ancient relic of a bygone. These top-performing televisions are my “desert island” picks, if said island had a power generator and good popcorn.

For more audio and home theater recommendations, check out related guides to the best OLED TVs, the best art TVs, the best RGB TVs, the best home theater projectors, and the best soundbars. If you truly don't know where to start, try our guide on how to buy a TV.

Update November 2026: We've revamped this entire guide, replacing nearly all of our top picks, Honorable Mentions, and Other TVs We've Tested.

The great debate: which size television is best for your living room? Does it even matter? The first thing to consider is price: an 80-inch TV is going to cost significantly more than a 65-inch one. In some cases, that means an extra grand or two for the privilege of seeing the stubble on Spider-Man’s face in great detail. Broadly speaking, the larger the room, the more useful a large screen is. The most popular size is 65 inches, which is a great option for most medium sizes spaces.

Recent findings suggest that I’m partial to art televisions for one simple reason: They are useful even when they are turned off. Art TVs use an antireflective layer on top of the screen to create more realistic, textured still images like artwork or paintings. The best ones can replace a picture frame or wall art in any room, and double as great TVs.

Should You Pick an OLED or RGB TV?

In a recent development, TV tech has evolved in 2026, and the new kid on the block is RGB TVs. These new models shine red, blue, and green light through an LCD panel to create brighter, more vibrant color. OLED on the other hand can control the color of individual pixels and even turn them off completely, leading to excellent contrast and black levels.

Which one performs the best? That depends. RGB models like the LG Micro RGB Evo provide more control over picture quality, brightness, and contrast. OLED televisions like the Samsung S95H tend to look better on movie night, especially for nighttime scenes when inky blacks need to look realistic. If pressed, I’d pick an RGB TV model because you get more control over color, but that's just me.

Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) Specs.

I picked Samsung's The Frame Pro (2026) as the best overall TV because it has stunningly good picture quality and looks incredible showcasing a masterpiece painting on your wall. I remember staring at the 65-inch model on the wall of my office for two months, just marveling at high-res shipwreck photos and the real wood bezels that encompass the screen (and snap easily into place, by the way). With just about every painting, The Frame Pro showed intricate and detailed textures, as though you could reach out and feel the waves of an ocean or curve of a face.

In a recent development, the Frame Pro is also an excellent choice for movies and shows. Because of the anti-glare screen and matte finish, the dark corridors of scenes in The Batman on HBO had extra depth and animated movies like Toy Story 5 on Disney+ popped with color. Sure, it doesn't have the true black pixels of an OLED screen, but its other capabilities more than make up for it.

According to recent reports, extra features included easy-to-install stands (no screws needed) and a breakout box called the Samsung Wireless One Connect that lets you connect streaming devices and a game console from across the room. That means fewer wires dangling on the wall.

TCL is a more budget-focused television maker that tends to undercut the price of brands like Samsung and LG. A good example of this is the TCL QM7L Mini-LED TV above, which has a budget-friendly price but anything but oriented picture quality. If anything, this QLED model competes with some OLED TVs for inky, deep blacks and rich color. Will you notice any contrast issues when you watch the latest Pixar film? Probably not, especially since the QM7L also looked exceptionally bright in our tests.

Sources indicate that A few other extras to mention: We loved the backlit remote, which makes it easier to punch up the volume or adjust picture quality settings in a dark room. You might even be able to skip a soundbar with this TV—the internal Bang & Olufsen speakers sound nice and loud.

Industry observers note that samsung, TCL, Hisense, and Sony released newly introduced RGB TVs this year, but it's the LG Micro RGB Evo that takes the crown, namely because you can tweak so many of its picture settings. In my tests,I could tweak the picture so much that movies and shows that mostly take place at night still looked visible, clear, and realistic. As one example among many, I remember tweaking settings for the movie Awake, a largely dark film, to the point where it looked clear and colorful. Other RGB models from Hisense and even Samsung struggled with those same dark scenes, no matter which setting I used.

In a recent development, another major plus is that this model supports 100 percent of the color gamut specs for BT.2020, DCI-P3, and Adobe RGB. In layman's terms, if you watch a movie like Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (which also matches those specs), you will see a true rainbow of every color available, with unmatched color vibrancy. This TV is so striking that I came away thinking that OLED TVs are no longer the obvious gold standard in 2026.

Samsung made a big change to their flagship OLED model this year, the Samsung S95H. They ditch the Samsung One Connect breakout box that was required with previous models (and is still required on TVs like The Frame Pro). The TV now has ports directly on the panel, where you can connect video game consoles, streaming devices, or Blu-ray players directly. While that might create more cable clutter, I found it much easier to use than the previous Samsung S95F.

Perhaps more importantly, the S95H is a top performer when it comes to picture quality and settings. I could adjust the contrast and brightness to perfectly light famously dim demonstrates like Game of Thrones. As an OLED, the blacks look richer and darker, more so than most RGB models. The AI optimization picture settings here are actually useful—during soccer matches, the TV adjust to make the pitch look even greener and minimizes background crowd noise, for example.

It's a bit pricey, but the overall brightness, contrast, color quality, and even built-in sound are all premium-grade.

According to recent reports, the firm famous for streaming sticks released its first OLED TV this year, and it follows the brand's formula of low-cost simplicity. Roku has, up until this point, stuck with LED TV models with average performance. Wonder of wonders, the Pro Series is not bad at all, making even dark scenes in movies like Solo: A Star Wars Story look vibrant and colorful. Outside of picture quality, Roku makes things as easy as possible, with features like Smart Picture Max, which automatically tweaks picture settings for you, a simple TV operating system (Roku OS, of course), and an uncluttered remote.

I will say, the brightness and contrast are good for this price, but nowhere near the cinema-quality color of something like the premium Samsung S95H. I think it's a great option for anyone on a budget or for people who only watch TV occasionally.

The Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) is my TV of the year, but the Amazon Ember Artline is also a capable, significantly cheaper, art TV. Just don't expert as premium of an image in movies and TV indicates.

Sources indicate that art televisions use a matte finish on the screen to help make paintings look more realistic and textured. The Ember Artline achieves this look, and even includes frame bezel that snap into place around the screen (these are sold separately on Samsung's Frame TVs). I loved looking at painting on this TV, including some animated ones Amazon offers in the catalog. Using the TV is simple, and the improved Alexa+ voice assistant is useful for changing the volume (hands free) or finding obscure sci-fi films.

Image quality isn't the big selling point of this TV: the art, aesthetic, and low price are. Gamers will find the 60 Hz refresh rate lacking, especially for twitchy action titles. Contrast and brightness are okay, but not nearly as impressive as something like the Samsung The Frame Pro. But keep in mind: this TV is far, far cheaper than premium options.

While the LG Micro RGB Evo is endlessly tweakable and outperformed every other RGB model I tested for picture quality, the Sony BRAVIA 9 II RGB TV still takes the cake when it comes to gaming. That’s especially true if you own a Sony PlayStation 5, since the TV will automatically adjust the picture quality and latency to match the game console. I tested it mostly using a high-end PC, and at a 120 Hz refresh rate, latency felt non-existent to me.

Sources indicate that I also found this TV to be a capable alternative to a premium OLED. Red, green, and blue colors are almost infinitely adjustable. During a scene in Toy Story 5 by a tree in a field, the sun creates splashes of color that look incredibly lush and vivid. Watching Game of Thrones, I found I could enable a special black level setting to make night battles look more realistic.

The Bravia 9 II uses Google TV OS and Google Gemini voice assistant, which both run simply, smoothly, and with no weird hiccups. While the LG Micro RGB Evo is a better performer for color and contrast, the BRAVIA 9 II’s gaming features, fast performance, high-end speakers, and deep blacks are exceptional.

Recent findings suggest that hisense UR9 RGB Mini-LED: My top pick for a midrange RGB, the Hisense UR9 has rich colors thanks to RGB tech shining red, green, and blue pixels. Some scenes, including ones in the movie The Last Duel, looked extra crisp and colorful. But it's not quite as excellent as my top picks.

It has been revealed that LG B6 OLED: The LG B6 is a great budget-friendly OLED TV that performed very similarly to the Roku Pro Series OLED. Either one of them would serve you well, but we gave the nod to the Roku TV for it's lower price, simpler remote, and easy to use Roku operating system.

Samsung Micro RGB R95H: Samsung's Micro RGB display tech didn’t make the Samsung Micro RGB R95H stand out from the competition as much as I'd hoped. In fact, the LG Micro RGB Evo responded much better to picture quality adjustments, and while reveals and movies looked colorful and clear, they weren't quite as jaw-dropping as similarly priced RGB and OLED competitors.

Sony Bravia 7 II: The Sony Bravia 7 II is unfortunately outclassed by the other midrange RGB TV on this list: the Hisense UR9. It is more expensive, it's harder to set up, and the picture quality doesn't quite match that of the Hisense TV.

Sources indicate that sony Bravia 8 II: Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata tested this stunning high-end OLED, and praised it's top-notch image quality and processing. That mentioned, the Samsung S95H is newer, about the same price, and has a more striking, glare-free image than the Sony Bravia 8 II.

Sources indicate that TCL Nxtvision Series Art: This budget art TV simply cannot compete with similarly low-priced art TVs like the Amazon Ember Artline TV and Hisense Class S7 CanvasTV. Both offer better picture quality and a better general user experience. You can read my full review here.

TCL RM9L RGB Mini-LED: The TCL RM9L RGB TV is huge and hugely expensive. The $6,000 85-inch is the smallest and cheapest model you can get, and it is generally outclassed by the LG Micro RGB Evo.

Sources indicate that the WIRED reviews team is busy testing the ever-popular midrange LG C6 and premium LG G6. Given past performances from LG C and G-series TVs, we expect them to be strong contenders for top accolades in this guide.

#128877. This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (902 w)

This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared.
  • Sources indicate that during the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different.
  • The newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared. The strange animal, an early relative of modern amphibians, has also received a name with a personal connection to the two student scientists who helped identify it.

Sources indicate that during the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different. Instead of a modern city, the landscape was a warm, swampy river delta populated by giant insects, early animals adapted to life on land, and unusual creatures swimming through its waterways. This environment supported an extraordinary variety of life, leaving behind fossils that now provide a remarkable glimpse into Earth's prehistoric past.

The newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog. Its name means "Jean's crawler from Mazon Creek," honoring the mothers of the two student researchers, both of whom are named Jean. The discovery is described in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

A 309-Million-Year-Old Fossil With Extraordinary Detail.

The Mazon Creek fossil deposits are among the world's most important sources of Carboniferous fossils, in large part because of the conditions that existed when the animals were alive.

Recent findings suggest that as plants and animals died in the ancient river delta, layers of sediment quickly covered their remains. This rapid burial created ideal conditions for fossilization, sometimes preserving delicate structures that would ordinarily disappear long before they could become fossils.

"What's really cool about Mazon Creek is that it preserves all of these unusual details -- things like toe pads and body outlines," indicates Allison Sefcovic, co-lead author of the paper and 2025 Women in Science intern at the Field.

"In the fossil of Jeanerpeton, we can see some of the scales on its back and tiny 'belly ribs' called gastralia. You can even see the eye impressions! It's so cool to see.".

These exceptionally preserved features offer valuable evidence of what early amphibian relatives looked like. They also indicate that several anatomical characteristics associated with modern frogs and salamanders were already present approximately 309 million years ago.

A Prehistoric Species Hidden in Plain Sight.

Industry observers note that although Jeanerpeton mazonensis has only recently been formally described, its fossil was discovered many years earlier. An amateur fossil collector originally found the specimen and later donated it to the Field Museum.

When researchers first examined it, they classified the animal as Amphibamus grandiceps, a previously established species known from the Mazon Creek area. However, closer examination eventually revealed that the fossil represented a distinct animal.

Misidentifications like this can occur when scientists have limited information about ancient species. Fossils that appear similar are sometimes assigned to an existing species even when important differences have not yet been recognized.

Paleontologists refer to such broad classifications as a "waste bin taxon." The term describes a category in which multiple fossils are grouped together because they seem related, even though their true identities and evolutionary relationships remain poorly understood.

"What we're finding from the Field Museum's collection are a bunch of things that historically were grouped together into this waste bin taxon known as Amphibamus grandiceps," says Cam So, co-author on the study and postdoctoral researcher at the Field Museum.

"Jeanerpeton is one of those species. And now, we've found enough evidence to support it being an anatomically distinct animal. With this publication, we officially pull Jeanerpeton out of this waste bin taxon.".

The finding highlights how museum collections can continue to produce discoveries long after fossils are first collected. In this case, a specimen already held by the Field Museum provided enough anatomical evidence to establish a separate species.

Two Student Scientists Make a Remarkable Discovery.

The research was co-led by Payton Kohlberg and Allison Sefcovic, who participated in the Field Museum's Women in Science internship program in 2025. The initiative encourages young women to explore careers in scientific research and museums.

Both students worked alongside So as members of the research group led by Arjan Mann, the museum's assistant curator of fossil fishes and early tetrapods in the Negaunee Integrative Research Center.

For Kohlberg, the project offered an opportunity to enter an unfamiliar scientific field and gain confidence through hands-on research.

"Before working in the Mann Lab, I didn't know much about paleontology," says Kohlberg. "My experience at the Field and in the Women in Science program has made me more confident in my abilities to try something fresh. It is scary to take on a project when you feel like you don't know as much as you should, but I learned with my practical experience that it is possible to overcome that fear with hard work.".

The identification of Jeanerpeton mazonensis adds another species to the growing record of ancient life preserved at Mazon Creek. As researchers continue examining fossils from the region, each discovery helps reveal more about the extraordinary diversity of animals and plants that inhabited Illinois more than 300 million years ago.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a city state, Singapore can often implement digital infrastructure projects more promptly than cities in much larger countries.Credit: Roslan Rahman/AFP via Getty Images.
  • Sources indicate that singapore is one of the world’s smallest countries by land area, spanning roughly 744 km2.
  • Sources indicate that the centralized government of Singapore, as a city-state, allows it to coordinate nationwide digital infrastructure projects with a speed and consistency that would be difficult in larger, more fragmented countries, says Orlando Woods, director of Singapore Management University’s Urban Institute, which studies urban growth and governance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a city state, Singapore can often implement digital infrastructure projects more promptly than cities in much larger countries.Credit: Roslan Rahman/AFP via Getty Images.

Sources indicate that singapore is one of the world’s smallest countries by land area, spanning roughly 744 km2. Yet as a technologically advanced city, it consistently punches above its weight. Earlier this year, Singapore placed ninth in the IMD Smart City Index 2026 — the highest-ranked city in Asia — noted for the strong trust its residents had in the government’s use of digital technologies. The index, published by IMD, a Swiss research institute, uses citizen surveys to evaluate cities’ physical and digital infrastructure across areas such as health and safety, governance and mobility.

Sources indicate that the centralized government of Singapore, as a city-state, allows it to coordinate nationwide digital infrastructure projects with a speed and consistency that would be difficult in larger, more fragmented countries, says Orlando Woods, director of Singapore Management University’s Urban Institute, which studies urban growth and governance. “It has a single layer of government,” says Woods. “To make decisions and implement things is just so much easier.”.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

In a recent development, singapore was among the earliest countries to digitize public services and integrate technological advancement across multiple government sectors, including health care, public services, transport and urban planning. In 2014, it announced these strategies as part of its ‘Smart Nation’ initiative, a major part of which is Virtual Singapore — one of the world’s first national-scale ‘digital twins’.

A dynamic, 3D replica of Singapore, the Virtual Singapore model encompasses everything from real-time air-quality statistics to population data and traffic flow. Comprising more than 100 TB of data collected from aerial photography, remote-sensing technologies and the thousands of sensors installed across the island, it is continually updated with latest geospatial, environmental and infrastructure data.

Sources indicate that local authorities use Virtual Singapore to inform urban-planning decisions, such as identifying the best rooftops for solar panels. It is also used in planning public-safety measures, including modelling flood impacts, drafting disaster-response aims and pinpointing potential risk areas for disease outbreaks, such as dengue fever. Some features and data sets are freely available to researchers, businesses and residents.
