💡 Key Takeaways
  • on Thursday unveiled Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec.
  • The retailer also stated Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.
  • Sources indicate that kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gap Inc. on Thursday unveiled Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

The retailer also stated Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.

Sources indicate that kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

Sources indicate that "I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter noted in a statement.

The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

Sources indicate that "Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode.".

Industry observers note that dickson said the tech giant is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.

While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson remarked this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.

In a recent development, gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.

It has been revealed that net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.

Gap also stated it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.

"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.

Industry observers note that at Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the organization attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. `.

Sources indicate that the firm's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.

"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson remarked.

The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its fresh CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the tech giant attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.

Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

Recent findings suggest that "We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth.".

Industry observers note that the International Film Festival Rotterdam (IFFR) Pro has unveiled the selection of 20 feature projects for the 44th edition of CineMart, its flagship co-production market, running Jan. 31-Feb. 3, as well as 10 projects for its work-in-progress platform Darkroom. And such big names as Aboriginal Australian filmmaker Warwick Thornton, Roma producer Nicolás Celis and North Macedonian auteur Teona Strugar Mitevska (God Exists, Her Name Is Petrunya) will be represented.Additionally, IFFR has shared the selected projects for the second edition of its Safe Harbour strand of CineMart for filmmakers who have experienced displacement or forced migration.IFFR Pro brings together filmmakers, producers and international industry partners around a carefully curated program of projects and opportunities. At its center is CineMart, which connects projects in development with potential partners and collaborators, alongside dedicated pathways for filmmakers supported by the Hubert Bals Fund and those participating in Safe Harbour. Darkroom extends this support to films approaching completion, while Rotterdam Lab invests in the next generation of producers and filmmakers. “Together, these initiatives reflect IFFR’s commitment to building lasting connections between artistic talent, international networks and the opportunities needed to bring distinctive cinematic visions to audiences,” organizers noted.“Among the notable filmmakers and producers featuring at CineMart 2027 are Caméra d’Or winner Warwick Thornton, Berlinale and Lux Audience Award winner Teona Strugar Mitevska, Nicolas Celis, producer of Academy Award-winning Roma and Emilia Perez, treble Cannes Critics’ Week winner Myroslav Slaboshpytskiy, Toronto Platform Award winner Carlos Marqués-Marcet and Tiger Award winner Paz Fábrega,” IFFR Pro said. Related Stories Movies Director Cédric Klapisch to Receive César Lifetime Achievement Honor Guest Column Bowen Yang, Mark Ruffalo and the Rise of Antisemitism in Hollywood (Guest Column).

Industry observers note that said Marten Rabarts, head of IFFR Pro: “From contemporary reinventions of the Western and working-class musical fables to personal and urgent stories of displacement and identity, this year’s CineMart, Darkroom and Safe Harbour selections unites an extraordinary range of cinematic voices – filmmakers reclaiming histories, subverting familiar genres and finding fresh ways to tell stories about our world. That we can bring together celebrated auteurs and festival alumni working in independent cinema with filmmakers embarking on their first features is something quintessentially Rotterdam. It is the strength, relevance and originality of the cinematic vision, rather than the stage of a filmmaker’s career, that draws us to a project.”.

A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it.
  • Sources indicate that researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger.
  • Industry observers note that observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a latest lease on life.

Sources indicate that researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.

Industry observers note that observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.

According to recent reports, "Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.".

How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion.

Recent findings suggest that for thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.

Recent findings suggest that once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly promptly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.

The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.

Recent findings suggest that "We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," remarked co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!".

Industry observers note that scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.

"When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," noted co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.".

A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome.

Industry observers note that this kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.

As the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.

It has been revealed that for Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.

But such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.

It has been revealed that these surviving systems are important because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.

Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.

Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb.

To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.

Sources indicate that the telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.

The simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.

Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Significant Bao.".

"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," remarked co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.

At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.

According to recent reports, further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Massive Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.

Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De mentioned.

The merger has left astronomers with another notable question: What is Bao like now?

The surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.

Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs.

One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.

According to recent reports, although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.

Industry observers note that the researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.).

The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.

It has been revealed that earlier records showed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.

By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) highlighted further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.

Another crucial development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.

It has been revealed that the telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.

Then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.

It has been revealed that scientists promptly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable new measurements.

According to recent reports, webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.

A Fresh Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars.

The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an crucial advance in the study of stellar mergers.

Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.

In a recent development, that timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.

The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.

NASA's recently debuted Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.

One of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.

With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar noted.

The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

Industry observers note that the James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever released, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.

Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.

A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.

Recent findings suggest that the studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov. 15, according to data from Rentrak. That's already roughly $290 million, or more than 50%, above its haul for all of 2025.

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the company's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

Industry observers note that when "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

Recent findings suggest that the company aims to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz mentioned on the company's earnings call earlier this month.

According to recent reports, paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

According to recent reports, the earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be important as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The firm has remarked it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

Breaking: German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Africa is a land of opportunity." "The German-African relationship is a win-win." "The continent is the market of the future.".
  • According to recent reports, that's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the sixth edition of the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana.
  • German firms are increasingly viewing Africa as an attractive destination as they scramble to find newly introduced markets amid wars in Ukraine and Iran, high energy prices, punishing US tariffs and slowing growth in traditional markets like China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Africa is a land of opportunity." "The German-African relationship is a win-win." "The continent is the market of the future.".

According to recent reports, that's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the sixth edition of the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana. While these descriptions aren't latest, there's a palpable sense of urgency and seriousness this time.

German firms are increasingly viewing Africa as an attractive destination as they scramble to find newly introduced markets amid wars in Ukraine and Iran, high energy prices, punishing US tariffs and slowing growth in traditional markets like China.

"For a long time, many German companies had a secure source of revenue from the major export markets in North America and China, but the geopolitical ruptures of our time have undermined this certainty," German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier stated during the event.

"One could also say that it is time for fresh horizons, time to take a closer look at economic opportunities still waiting for us.".

Africa is home to some of the fastest growing economies in the world, like Ethiopia and Rwanda. Even as European and other advanced economies contend with declining working-age populations, Africa is expected to add hundreds of millions of workers in the next few decades, emerging as a key source of future labor.

Germany has already signed a migration pact with Kenya and is working on one with Ghana as it seeks to attract skilled workers to help ease acute labor shortages in certain sectors at home.

Even as Africa remains one of the poorest regions in the world, economic growth in parts of the continent has created a larger and more affluent consumer class over the past three decades. This group is aspirational and a growing source of demand for many of the goods that German firms want to sell, from cars to cosmetics.

The continent, with its mineral wealth and renewable energy potential, is central to European Union efforts to diversify its sources of critical raw materials and reduce reliance on China-dominated supply chains.

It is also playing an increasingly important role in strengthening the EU's energy security after the bloc phased out most energy imports from Russia.

German firms have committed to invest billions of euros in green hydrogen projects in countries such as Mauritania and Namibia.

"We don't have the capital to develop them [natural resources]. So foreign investors are coming to help us develop those resources. Whilst we are getting jobs and industrialization is taking place, they are also making profits," said Amin Amidu Sulemani, energy and infrastructure commissioner at the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).

"It's not a relationship where we send raw materials outside of Africa every time, when we can actually process them here," he told DW.

Despite Africa's growing economic appeal, many obstacles to investment remain, including corruption and governance concerns, unreliable energy supplies, foreign exchange risk and poor infrastructure.

African leaders say they are working to address these challenges and improve the ease of doing business.

Yet while German companies have largely remained on the sidelines, competitors from countries such as the UAE, Turkey and India have made significant inroads across the continent.

German firms enjoy a strong reputation in Africa because of their engineering expertise, vocational training programs and long-term industrial investments, which are more likely to create stable jobs than investments in extractive industries.

Industry observers note that however, they have struggled to translate that goodwill into a larger commercial presence. Africa, for instance, accounts for less than 2% of the total foreign investment made by German firms over the past several decades.

Business leaders complain that German firms lack adequate financing and risk protection for projects in Africa. They also criticize excessive bureaucracy and the absence of a coherent German strategy, with engagement fragmented across ministries and agencies.

Industry bodies say German institutions and firms often perceive risks too broadly, treating diverse African markets as if they pose the same level of risk.

"German companies can be a bit more bold and maybe also innovative in the way they approach the continent," Khadi Camara, deputy CEO of the German-African Business Association, told DW. "We see that in the companies that are successful, they don't do business as usual. Every country has its nuances that companies keep in mind and say, okay, this model works here, that model works there.".

The 2026 World Investment Report by UN trade body UNCTAD highlighted that investors from the Gulf and Asia are becoming crucial sources of investment in Africa, especially in energy, logistics, real estate and infrastructure.

The UAE has been a major investor in greenfield megaprojects in recent years, including the $34 billion (€31 billion) Infinity Power renewable energy project in Mauritania, the $24 billion Ras El Hikma real estate development project in Egypt and the $6 billion H2 Global Energy hydrogen project in Tunisia.

Business leaders are calling for better financing and guarantees, and more risk-sharing and fewer bureaucratic hurdles.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, others, including the German president, are urging German businesses to take on more risk and seize opportunities in Africa. Otherwise, they risk being edged out by foreign rivals.

"Be curious, take risks and invest in our common future," Steinmeier mentioned.

The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.
  • The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.
  • It has been revealed that wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

It has been revealed that wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had debuted aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

It has been revealed that hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a newly introduced class of NASA astronauts.

He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s so much more than the four names that have been announced,” Glover said during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”.

Recent findings suggest that glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which introduced to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

In a recent development, koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

Recent findings suggest that the Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

Recent findings suggest that if all goes to strategy, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton mentioned via email.

After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

According to recent reports, artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

Sources indicate that the Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already remarked delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

The space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

Recent findings suggest that vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

Sources indicate that “I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche said. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

Koch noted in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

“We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch stated. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”.

She stated the offer rendered her “speechless.”.

“It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”.

An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.

Breaking: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen.
  • In a recent development, quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility.
  • Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

In a recent development, quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.

According to recent reports, now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times.".

Industry observers note that atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Recent findings suggest that modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A New Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

"It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a fresh technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.".

That improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A Fresh Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity.

The findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening newly introduced possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

For now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

It has been revealed that "Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the big next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.".

If successful, such experiments could offer scientists a new way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

  • Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit.
  • "This action opens a bold newly introduced frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr mentioned today (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit.

"This action opens a bold newly introduced frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr mentioned today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval.

AI has become central to SpaceX's business aims and identity over the past year or so. For example, the tech giant has said that it's eyeing a "total addressable market" of $28.5 trillion over the long haul — and nearly $23 trillion of that is in "enterprise AI applications.".

Starmind is key to those lofty ambitions. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk believes that the future of AI compute is in space, where energy (from the sun) is unlimited and there are no land-owning neighbors to lodge NIMBY complaints.

Sources indicate that spaceX aims to launch the first of its Starmind satellites in the third quarter of 2027. The spacecraft will fly on the firm's fully reusable Starship megarocket, which has deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink satellites on its most recent two test flights.

Those 52 spacecraft are the vanguard of another enormous constellation: Musk has said that the next-gen Starlink network will eventually consists of about 100,000 satellites.

The planned numbers for Starlink and Starmind are truly mind-boggling. To put them into perspective: Since the dawn of the space age in 1957, humanity has launched a total of just 28,000 satellites, give or take a few hundred. And the biggest constellation ever operated to date, the current iteration of Starlink, consists of about 11,000 spacecraft.

It has been revealed that these coming buildouts will require an enormous number of launches. Starship can carry a maximum of 60 V3 Starlink satellites per launch, for instance, so it will take about 1,700 liftoffs just to assemble that network (and more to maintain it, as the operational life of each satellite is expected to be about five years).

Putting so many satellites into orbit also raises the risks of collisions. SpaceX has proven to be extremely proficient in this regard with its current Starlink satellites, which can detect and avoid potential collisions autonomously. But more evasive maneuvers will be required as space gets more and more crowded.

SpaceX isn't the only firm that aims to operate data centers in space; Cowboy Space, Starcloud, Blue Origin and Google, among other companies, have voiced similar ambitions. Starcloud and Google, in fact, have already launched AI pathfinder satellites.

"Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America's leadership in SI," Carr remarked in the same statement. ("SI" stands for super intelligence, the Trump administration's preferred term for AI.).

"By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," Carr added. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.".

In a recent development, hammond appeared on Times Radio on Wednesday to discuss the series, shortly after it was revealed that Gordon Ramsay would be taking the wheel as lead presenter. Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations.
  • Sources indicate that the study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy.
  • Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

Sources indicate that the study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

"This idea that relativity is important in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," said Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements.".

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds.

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

Atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

In a recent development, some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

The sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

It has been revealed that for lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

Heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become important, changing how the electrons behave.

One particularly crucial effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

"The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang remarked. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.".

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds.

According to recent reports, to test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

Industry observers note that bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

The researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

Sources indicate that by measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

It has been revealed that rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks.

It has been revealed that the findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

Bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang stated.

In a recent development, the research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The sequel to “Bandit Queen,” the 1994 drama about Indian outlaw Phoolan Devi, is aiming for a release at the end of 2027 or early 2028, producer Bobby Bedi tells Variety, with the screenplay now in its final draft and casting underway.
  • Bedi, who produced Shekhar Kapur’s original, is calling the follow-up “Bandit Queen MP.” Honey Trehan, director of the Diljit Dosanjh-starrer “Satluj,” was unveiled as director earlier this month.
  • The latest film picks up where Kapur’s ended, following Devi from her years in prison to her assassination, and a little beyond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The sequel to “Bandit Queen,” the 1994 drama about Indian outlaw Phoolan Devi, is aiming for a release at the end of 2027 or early 2028, producer Bobby Bedi tells Variety, with the screenplay now in its final draft and casting underway.

Bedi, who produced Shekhar Kapur’s original, is calling the follow-up “Bandit Queen MP.” Honey Trehan, director of the Diljit Dosanjh-starrer “Satluj,” was unveiled as director earlier this month. Related Stories Mike Newell Recalls Being Shot at in Colombia While Filming ‘Love in the Time of Cholera’ With Giovanna Mezzogiorno: ‘She Was Like, “F— All This!”’.

The latest film picks up where Kapur’s ended, following Devi from her years in prison to her assassination, and a little beyond.

Recent findings suggest that “The film is really about the tumultuous love story of a married man and a prisoner negotiating their lives in this ‘even more dangerous’ landscape through freedom, fame and fortune. But to what end?” Bedi notes.

He adds that women’s role in politics is back at the forefront, and that Devi was a soldier for the cause in her day.

In a recent development, “My first film was about the rape and revenge and fate of a lower caste woman in India’s rural landscape. This film happens to be the story of the political power and ultimate fate of a low caste woman in the urban political landscape. It just happens to be the same woman,” he claims.

Bedi describes the project as latest territory for both him and Trehan.

Trehan worked on Bedi’s 2003 production “Maqbool,” directed by Vishal Bhardwaj, and the producer notes the maturity of his later independent work stood out. “And then came ‘Satluj,’ earlier called ‘Punjab ’95.’ It blew me over. Well researched, superbly cast, well directed. Very impressive. He is clearly a perfectionist,” Bedi says.

Sources indicate that “Satluj,” in which Dosanjh plays human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra, spent nearly four years in India’s certification process. Originally titled “Ghallughara,” it was cleared by the Central Board of Film Certification with 21 cuts and an enforced title change to “Punjab ’95,” and was pulled from the gala slot it had been set for at the 2023 Toronto International Film Festival. The film finally premiered uncut on ZEE5 Global on July 3 this year. Less than two days later, ZEE5 took it down in India, saying it would be “unavailable in India until further notice.” Days after that, the platform removed it from its international catalogue as well.

Trehan indicates “Bandit Queen” inspired filmmakers of his generation, and that being asked by Bedi to carry its legacy forward is special. He is right now absorbed in the material and the research Bedi has already done, and has known the producer since his Delhi theater days, before “Maqbool.”.

“He is such a hands-on producer,” Trehan says.

Phoolan Devi’s story has already returned to the screen this year with Richie Mehta’s “Phoolan,” from Amazon MGM Studios and Namah Pictures, which premiered at the Toronto Film Festival. Rather than retell her whole life, the film, starring Sneha Kumari, centers on a 48-hour siege of a village by 2,000 police and paramilitary personnel sent to capture her when she was 17.

#128755. Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something substantial about the Big Bang

Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something substantial about the Big Bang

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in the earliest moments after the Big Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma.
  • Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators.
  • Recent findings suggest that one way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the earliest moments after the Big Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma. Temperatures reached trillions of degrees, and quarks and gluons raced through this primordial soup at nearly the speed of light. This extreme state of matter existed for only a few microseconds before quarks began combining into the more stable protons and neutrons that eventually helped form the matter around us.

Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators. By colliding ions at speeds approaching that of light, they produce tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma about the size of an atomic nucleus. Each droplet survives for only tens of septillionths of a second, giving researchers an incredibly brief opportunity to investigate the substance that filled the newborn universe.

Recent findings suggest that one way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it. Although these particles are not part of the surrounding plasma being studied, their movements can reveal important details about its microscopic structure. This approach builds on a principle first described by Albert Einstein in 1905.

However, Einstein's original framework has limitations under the extraordinary conditions found in quark-gluon plasma. When particles approach the speed of light, interactions occur that his theory does not fully account for.

MIT Physicists Extend Einstein's Century-Old Theory.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have now developed a theoretical framework that goes beyond Einstein's original description. Their work predicts how a fluid affects particles traveling at relativistic speeds, including the forces that accelerate, slow, and redirect them.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers believe their calculations could help scientists better understand how heavy quarks move through quark-gluon plasma. By comparing their predictions with results from particle accelerator experiments, physicists may be able to uncover new details about the internal structure of this ancient form of matter and the conditions that prevailed shortly after the Big Bang.

"Our result reveals a upcoming source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion," states Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute. "How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside.".

In a recent development, du Plessis conducted the research with Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB. Their findings were published in Physical Review Letters.

How Pollen in Water Inspired Einstein's Discovery.

It has been revealed that the origins of this research stretch back nearly two centuries to an observation made by botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown noticed that pollen grains suspended in apparently motionless water moved unpredictably, constantly shifting and drifting despite the absence of any visible disturbance. Scientists eventually named this phenomenon "Brownian motion.".

Einstein provided a scientific explanation in 1905, showing that these seemingly random movements were caused by tiny, invisible interactions between particles suspended in a fluid and the atoms and molecules surrounding them.

Recent findings suggest that he demonstrated that two competing effects govern the movement of a particle through a fluid. The first is drag, which resists the particle's movement and slows it down. The second consists of countless random pushes from the surrounding atoms and molecules. Although individual microscopic particles are extremely small, their combined activity can deliver enough energy to make larger particles move unpredictably.

Einstein's theory established a relationship between these effects, allowing scientists to learn about the microscopic properties of a fluid by studying the motion of particles inside it.

Industry observers note that over the following decades, researchers applied this principle to many different fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They generally expected particles traveling through such plasma to experience a balance of drag and random impacts resembling the behavior of pollen grains in water.

Industry observers note that in conventional Brownian motion, the likelihood of different forces follows a bell-shaped curve. Moderate pushes are the most common (the highest point of the bell), while unusually strong pushes in either direction are much less likely (the tail ends of the bell). Over time, the balance of drag and random motion allows a particle to reach the same temperature as its surroundings.

But this familiar description becomes incomplete when particles move at speeds approaching that of light.

According to recent reports, "Einstein revealed that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings," Du Plessis explains. "For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we've known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did.".

Unexpected Forces Reveal Hidden Physics in Quark-Gluon Plasma.

To investigate what Einstein's traditional model was missing, Du Plessis and Scheihing-Hitschfeld calculated how a heavy quark would respond to the forces inside a fluid while moving close to the speed of light.

Their calculations focused on the strong nuclear force, one of nature's fundamental forces, which governs interactions between quarks and gluons and holds them together.

The team began with a relatively simple model consisting of a gas of quarks and gluons that interacted only weakly with one another. Starting with these weaker interactions made it possible to calculate the forces acting on a heavy quark passing through the gas.

It has been revealed that they then determined how those forces would change the quark's momentum as it moved. A stronger push produces a larger change in momentum, so the calculations allowed the researchers to predict the likelihood of impacts of different strengths.

Sources indicate that at first, the resulting probability curve looked similar to the bell-shaped distribution associated with Einstein's theory. For small changes in momentum, the familiar pattern still held. But when the researchers examined larger changes, they discovered a striking difference.

Instead of the expected symmetrical curve, the distribution was tilted, with unequal probabilities for extreme changes in opposite directions. Powerful impacts occurred more frequently than the traditional Brownian model predicted, and unusually large slowdowns were more likely than similarly large increases in speed.

Recent findings suggest that "The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare," Du Plessis states. "For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected.".

A Universal Pattern Could Reveal the Universe's First Fluid.

The researchers next examined whether this unusual behavior depended on the particular particles making up the plasma.

They repeated their calculations using plasmas containing different types of particles and found that the same tilted distribution appeared regardless of the composition.

Sources indicate that even more intriguingly, they recognized the same underlying pattern in an earlier calculation involving strongly coupled plasma, where particles interact much more intensely with one another. Despite the substantial differences in microscopic behavior between the two types of plasma, the probability distributions shared the same distinctive structure.

This suggested that the researchers had identified a potentially universal feature of how fast-moving particles interact with fluids, rather than an effect confined to one particular model.

In a recent development, "This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized," Du Plessis indicates. "This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks.".

The discovery could offer physicists a valuable new tool for investigating the extraordinarily hot matter that dominated the universe immediately after the Big Bang. By studying the rare, extreme changes in the movement of heavy quarks, scientists may be able to learn more about the interactions occurring deep inside quark-gluon plasma.

Industry observers note that the results also point toward an crucial characteristic of this primordial substance. Rather than behaving like a relatively loose collection of particles, the universe's first fluid may have been governed by much stronger interactions than a conventional Brownian motion model would indicate.

Industry observers note that du Plessis suggests that primordial quark-gluon plasma was likely "more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It's more like a liquid and less like a gas.".

By extending a theory Einstein developed more than a century ago, the researchers have opened a promising new approach to studying one of the most extreme states of matter in nature and potentially uncovering what the universe was like during its first fleeting moments.

Industry observers note that the research received partial support from the Office of Nuclear Physics within the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation.

SpaceX Starship debris becomes art in Ashley Zelinskie's 'The Weight of Space' (video, photos)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan.
  • Look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Starship print is part of "Ejecta," which captures rocket plumes and explosions on paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan. 2025, pieces of its heat shield washed ashore. Some of that material now hangs on a gallery wall in Newly introduced York City, embedded in artist Ashley Zelinskie's print of the very explosion it survived.

Look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface. Some of Zelinskie's friends vacationing on the islands had come across pieces of heat-shield tile. "I think you might want these," Zelinskie recalled one friend telling her. She did. The Brooklyn-based artist ground the fragments into dust and worked them into the print.

Recent findings suggest that the Starship print is part of "Ejecta," which captures rocket plumes and explosions on paper. It's one of four series in Zelinskie's solo exhibition, "The Weight of Space," which opened Nov. 20 at Heft Gallery in Manhattan. Her marble sculptures in "Monuments" depict the Hubble Space Telescope, retired NASA astronaut Mike Massimino's spaceflight gear and more. Five "Launch Sequence" sculptures follow a rocket through liftoff, and the interactive "Crowded Sky" lets visitors track what's currently orbiting overhead in real time.

According to recent reports, zelinskie gave Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik and me a tour before the gallery doors opened. Massimino joined her that evening to celebrate the exhibition and their collaboration on "Monuments." You can watch the tour in the video above.

Recent findings suggest that massimino turned up in our first look at Zelinskie's work, too. In 2022, I photographed the two of them beside her "Exploration JWST" sculpture at "Unfolding the Universe: First Light," an exhibit inspired by the James Webb Space Telescope's first images. Four years later, Massimino stood in a New York gallery looking at another Zelinskie sculpture. "That's my arm there," he told Malik.

In that hand is a piece of hardware Malik remembers watching Massimino wrestle with in real time. During NASA's final Hubble servicing mission in 2009, a stripped bolt left a handrail blocking access to the telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS). Mission Control instructed Massimino to forcibly remove the handrail so he and fellow spacewalker Michael Good could get on with the repair.

Massimino told Malik that pulling the handrail off Hubble brought back a childhood memory of his father and his Uncle Frank driving a long screwdriver through a stuck oil filter. "Then my uncle Frank pulled to get more leverage, and that's what was going through my mind when I pulled off that handrail," Massimino mentioned. He remembered looking down at Earth and thinking, "This one's for you, Uncle Frank.".

Sources indicate that massimino wore bulky, pressurized gloves to pull off the handrail, but Zelinskie chose to show his bare hand gripping the copper-plated replica. "I wanted to bring the humanity back into the piece," she told Malik.

The gloves have a story of their own. When Massimino brought a pair to her studio to be 3D-scanned, Zelinskie noticed how the fabric held its folds when the gloves were set down. "Oh my god, these want to be stone," she recalled thinking. So she went out and learned to work in marble.

Sources indicate that the astronaut boots have a detail you could easily miss from above. Zelinskie polished the soles smooth because, as she put it, "they're built for floating in space." For her sculpture of Massimino's reentry helmet, the kind he wore for the trip home from space, Zelinskie paired carved marble with a 3D-printed visor, which she electroplated and polished to a mirror finish.

The Hubble Space Telescope gets its own marble tribute in "Monuments." Zelinskie started with a NASA 3D model of the telescope and used the modeling software Blender to give it a veil.

According to recent reports, "So I kind of threw a digital piece of fabric on the Hubble telescope over and over and over again until I got it right," she told Malik. The veil is a nod to the blurry images Hubble first sent back to Earth. A Digital Stone Project robotic arm in Tuscany carved the rough shape in marble, and Zelinskie finished it by hand. When she invited Malik to touch what looked like cloth, he reached out. "It's like a very buttery, smooth surface," he said.

Sources indicate that the last time we saw Zelinskie at Heft, she and DJ and producer illich Mujica had filled the gallery with Webb imagery, live electronic music and a little Pink Floyd for their audiovisual performance "Redshift." We've also seen her turn Webb's view of the Pillars of Creation into artwork. This time, one of the images on the wall began with a camera Zelinskie pointed at a rocket herself.

Industry observers note that zelinskie photographed NASA's Artemis 2 launch from the Kennedy Space Center visitor center in Florida. The resulting print is part of "Ejecta," alongside the Starship breakup print and more. She uses data to distort the image until the swirls in a rocket plume start to resemble a nebula.

Another print in the series depicts the loss of the space shuttle Challenger. That one has a personal connection for me. Jan. 28, 1986, was my birthday. Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff that day, killing all seven crew members. The memory of that day helped inspire my career covering space.

Industry observers note that massimino spoke with Malik about what it was like to see a familiar image of the disaster through Zelinskie's eyes. "It's an artist's interpretation of it, which in some way, when I look at it, is more emotional," he mentioned.

Sources indicate that "I just became obsessed with launch clouds," Zelinskie told Malik. That fascination made its way into "Launch Sequence," a series of five sculptures that capture successive moments of liftoff.

The cloud grows as the rocket climbs away. For the shape of the rocket itself, Zelinskie drew on sculptor Constantin Brâncuși's "Bird in Space" to give it the feeling of upward motion.

Sources indicate that the tour ends with "Crowded Sky," where visitors can follow individual objects in Earth orbit. White markers represent government-owned objects and black markers represent privately owned ones. When the display picks out a target, scan a QR code and your phone tells you what you're looking at, what it does and when it released.

Wind the clock back far enough and there's just one object to follow. Run it a decade into the future and you get Zelinskie's projection of how much busier the sky could become.

With all those objects circling overhead, Malik asked Zelinskie what space means to her. "I think the more we learn about space, the more we appreciate our own planet," she said. "It's the overview effect. And I'm hoping that everybody gets that out of the artwork.".

Sources indicate that "The Weight of Space" runs through Jan. 16, 2027, at Heft Gallery in Upcoming York City. Explore more of Zelinskie's work on the artist's website.

He is also the producer/writer/editor of Space.com's CosMix series on space-enthused artists. He studied psychology at the State University of New York at Stony Brook and is originally from Zadar, Croatia by way of Astoria, NY. Latest Update: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space.
  • Fresh research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes.
