📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

Fresh research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

It has been revealed that the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Sources indicate that despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

Sources indicate that to investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Recent findings suggest that even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

In a recent development, "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

It has been revealed that the researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

Sources indicate that finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

In a recent development, "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

It has been revealed that by studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The newly introduced findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

According to recent reports, the research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At first glance, everything seems to be business as usual.
  • "As a country, we are in a difficult situation geopolitically, technologically, and demographically, and next year's budget is an accurate reflection of that," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) acknowledged on Wednesday in the Bundestag.
  • "If we don't change course, in a few years we'll find ourselves in a situation where all federal revenue will have to be spent on social programs, interest payments, and defense," he reflected on Wednesday during a four-hour debate focused on government policy as a whole, rather than the individual budgets of the ministries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, everything seems to be business as usual. Lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, are holding four days of final debates on how much money the federal government may spend in the coming year, and on what. These follow a familiar pattern: The government pats itself on the back, while the opposition voices criticism. But anyone listening more closely will notice that there are doubts even in the ranks of the coalition parties, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), their Bavarian allies, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

"As a country, we are in a difficult situation geopolitically, technologically, and demographically, and next year's budget is an accurate reflection of that," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) acknowledged on Wednesday in the Bundestag.

"If we don't change course, in a few years we'll find ourselves in a situation where all federal revenue will have to be spent on social programs, interest payments, and defense," he reflected on Wednesday during a four-hour debate focused on government policy as a whole, rather than the individual budgets of the ministries.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This government has now been in office for about 20 months. Back in early 2025, expectations were enormous. Merz had promised to bring the budget back in line with the debt brake enshrined in the constitution, which stipulates that the government can spend only slightly more than it collects (with exceptions now made for defense and security).

Yet for 2027, spending — at just under €561 billion ($614 billion) — will be higher than ever before, and tax revenues are nowhere near sufficient to cover this, meaning Germany is looking at record borrowing for the year totaling €210 billion.

The largest opposition party, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) calculated that the government will incur €401,000 in upcoming debt every minute next year. In the Bundestag, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla called it a "debt orgy" that will paralyze the country. Merz will "go down in history as the chancellor who led Germany to bankruptcy," he exclaimed.

Industry observers note that germany's budget deficit has only ever been higher in the COVID-19 pandemic. The current pressures are obvious: The economy is struggling, the population aging, and Russia's war against Ukraine is about to enter its sixth year.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The defense budget is now by far the highest in the history of the Federal Republic, with €109 billion allocated for 2027, an increase of €27 billion on last year. Added to this is the multi-year, debt-financed special military fund, intended to modernize the armed forces, bringing the total defense budget to €139 billion.

Sources indicate that the AfD and the socialist Left Party have sharply criticized this. Left Party parliamentary leader Heidi Reichinnek accused the government of pursuing "militarization and boundless rearmament on the one hand, and brutal social cuts and an orgy of budget cuts on the other.".

The AfD's Chrupalla stated that the temporary reduction in the electricity tax, pushed through at the last minute, would save the average family a mere €100 a year, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "walks out of the chancellery here in Berlin with a check for €200 million after just one afternoon.".

It has been revealed that "Whose chancellor are you, Mr. Merz?" he asked.

The opposition Greens did not agree. While they also criticized the budget as "unserious," Green Party Bundestag member Britta Haßelmann described the AfD's stance on Ukraine as shameful. She rejected the idea that money was being wasted on Ukraine, saying that supporting Ukraine bolstered security for Germany and Europe.

It has been revealed that the chancellor shares this view. "You can't say it often enough, either to the far right or the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than just Ukraine," Merz mentioned.

He added that Russia is escalating tensions in the Baltic region, in Poland, in the Black Sea, and in space; and that Moscow is also seeking escalation in Germany, even at the cost of lives. "That is why we must show Russia its limits," he remarked.

Industry observers note that but it is becoming increasingly difficult for the government to justify the high spending on Ukraine. Germany's pension and health care costs are only getting bigger: By far the largest single budget item is that of the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is rising to over €200 billion, even with cuts to unemployment benefits.

It has been revealed that work is right now underway on a reform of the pension system — something that many see as urgent, as the workforce born in the 1960s, when more than a million children were born in Germany every year, is on brink of retiring. Birth rates nearly halved by the mid-1970s and declined even further afterward. For now, so-called "boomers" still make up one-third of the current workforce — but soon they will be drawing pensions.

Recent findings suggest that even now, Germany's pensions cannot be financed solely with contributions on wages and salaries. In 2025, just over €420 billion in pensions were paid out, with the government contributing €127 billion of that amount. By 2027, the government aims to save €3 billion on this figure, which is likely to further increase pension contributions.

The coalition parties are stuck in a row over how to reform the pension system. Chancellor Merz insisted in the Bundestag that the coalition was solving the country's fundamental problems, but he warned that in future, tax revenues "will no longer be enough to afford everything we have become all too accustomed to," he said. "All of us here will have to give up some of the ideas we cherish.".

The SPD, on the other hand, is counting on increasing federal revenue. Its parliamentary leader Matthias Miersch emphasized in the Bundestag that large fortunes and inheritances must contribute more to "public costs.".

That, he stated, must also apply to large companies. Currently, heirs to family-owned businesses often pay significantly less in taxes than heirs to real estate or financial assets, because they can be exempted from inheritance tax if they continue to run the business. This is intended to protect them from having to pay taxes in the event of a breakup or sale of the tech giant.

Industry observers note that according to Miersch, the government must now think about taxing the wealthy more. "For us, this concern is by no means off the table; on the contrary, we are putting it on the agenda," he said. The government's revenue situation is "an issue we need to discuss.".

Sources indicate that all in all, the outlook for 2027 is strained — and not just financially. The political differences between the CDU/CSU and the SPD are likely to make working together even more difficult. Conflict is inevitable, especially with several state elections scheduled for the spring.

The chancellor knows this and tried to appear confident that better collaboration was possible. "We must seek compromise in our joint decision-making, represented by these — admittedly quite different — coalition partners," he said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Best International Oscar race is the biggest ever — a record 104 international features are in contention, beating the previous high-water mark of 93 set in 2020 — and one of the most open in years.

There is no out-and-out favorite this season, although European cinema again looks strong, with Javier Calvo and Javier Abrosso’s Spanish entry La Bola Negra; Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord, in the running for Romania; and Pawel Pawlikowski’s Polish contender Fatherland all expected to make the short list, alongside Asian faves including South Korea’s Possible Love, from Lee Chang-dong; and Japan’s All of a Sudden from Ryusuke Hamaguchi.

Behind that top five is a long list of maybes, including French entry Minotaur from twice-nominated Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev; Lukas Dhont’s WWI drama Coward, Belgium’s entry; Austria’s Rose, which like Fatherland stars Sandra Huller; and Rehearsals for a Revolution, Pegah Ahangarani’s documentary on her family and their battles against the Iranian regime, which is the U.K. official Oscar submission.

Recent findings suggest that one hundred films were submitted by countries or regions. Four qualified through a newly introduced method where movies that win top awards at leading festivals are accepted as long as they meet the language, creative input and theatrical-release requirements for the category. According to Academy rules, an international feature film is defined as a feature-length motion picture (more than 40 minutes) produced outside the United States with a predominantly (more than 50 percent) non-English dialogue track. New Zealand’s submission, Taratoa Stappard’s gothic horror tale Mārama, was dropped for falling short of the language requirement.

Recent findings suggest that academy members from all branches who meet the minimum viewing requirements can participate in the preliminary round of voting for the shortlist, taking place between will take place Dec. 7-11. The shortlist of 15 international films will be revealed on Dec. 15. Oscar nominations voting will take place Jan. 11-15, 2027, with the nominations announcement on Jan. 21.

The 99th Academy Awards will be held on March 14, 2027.

In a recent development, THR has exhaustively compiled the full list of international contenders, with trailers, reviews and talent interviews where available. Enjoy!

Roland Sejko’s documentary uses archival footage, newsreels and state-produced cinema to examine how Enver Hoxha’s communist regime used film as an instrument of propaganda. Tracing Albania’s isolation and political transformation over four decades, the film explores how the country’s official image was manufactured, controlled and disseminated by the state.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Sources indicate that in 1993, a car crash leaves Ahmed amnesiac, so that not even his family feels familiar. His youngest son fears him and his bandaged face, while Ahmed feels uneasy about his neighbor. Yanis Koussim’s debut feature — the Arabic title means “exorcism” — reimagines the traumas of Algeria’s bloody “Black Decade” (1992–2002), a civil war between the government and Islamist rebel groups, as a horror film, blending memory, trauma and possession.

It has been revealed that teenage angst meets the supernatural in Laura Casabé’s coming-of-age horror film, set over a single lazy summer day in 2001, at the peak of Argentina’s great depression. Amid the backdrop of social unrest, adolescent desire turns deadly in this slow-burn rage thriller, which debuted at Sundance in 2025.

According to recent reports, tamara Stepanyan’s narrative feature debut follows Céline, a French woman who travels to Armenia to settle the affairs of her supposedly deceased husband, Arto. There she discovers that he concealed his past as a soldier and is regarded by some as a deserter. As she investigates his life, Céline encounters a country still haunted by successive wars and their unresolved consequences.

Read THR‘s interview with director Tamara Stepanyan here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

James J. Robinson’s debut feature is the country’s first-ever Tagalog-language submission for the Oscars. The meditative film focuses on an aging woman who questions her faith as the world crumbles around her. After a young construction worker dies under suspicious circumstances, an elderly nun whose life has been shaped by discipline, service and belief, gets drawn into a world of crime and corruption.

The trailer for First Light is below.

It has been revealed that sandra Hüller is everywhere in this season’s awards conversation, but the German star gives her most transformative performance playing a 17th-Century woman passing as a male farmer in Markus Schleinzer’s period drama. Hüller won the Best Performance trophy in Berlin for the role, which was based on hundreds of similar recorded cases throughout history. Read THR’s review of Rose here.

Zaur Gasimli’s historical drama follows Azerbaijani philanthropist Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev and his efforts to establish Baku’s first school for Muslim girls in 1901. Facing fierce opposition from religious conservatives, Taghiyev enlists the support of his young wife, Sona, in a campaign that becomes a test of his influence, diplomacy and determination to expand educational opportunities for women.

Sources indicate that mejbaur Rahman Sumon reimagines Adam and Eve in the monsoon-soaked Bengali countryside in this dark folk tale. A tenant farmer (Mostafizur Noor Imran) wants out of his arranged marriage to a woman (Nazifa Tushi) the villagers regard as insane. Promising her a trip to the circus, he rows her into the forest and slips away in the dark. Yet however far he takes her, the thud of a palm fruit beside their hut announces her return. Sumon’s follow-up to Hawa, Bangladesh’s 2022 Oscar submission, premiered in Rotterdam’s Tiger Competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

Lukas Dhont’s queer World War I drama follows two Belgian soldiers, Pierre and Francis, who find an unexpected refuge from the brutality of the trenches in the world of theatre. Assigned to organize entertainment for their fellow troops, the men develop an increasingly intimate relationship as they put together a revue behind the front lines. Leads Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne shared the Best Actor prize at Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

It has been revealed that this Turkish-language political drama from German Academy Award nominee İlker Çatak (The Teacher’s Lounge) qualified for Oscar submission by winning the Golden Bear for Best Film at the Berlinale. Özgü Namal and Tansu Biçer star as Derya and Aziz, a successful theatrical couple whose lives are upended after their latest production brings them into conflict with the authorities in Ankara. Dismissed from their jobs and forced to leave their home, they find their loss of professional standing and financial security puts their marriage under pressure, testing the convictions that once united them.

Read THR‘s interview with Çatak here and THR‘s review of Yellow Letters here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Industry observers note that the coming-of-age drama about tradition, ambition and choosing your own destiny follows a young woman in the Bolivian Andes who takes up the sacred ways of midwifery, but dreams of escaping to the city to become a singer. Directed by Álvaro Olmos Torrico, The Condor Daughter had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival.

Recent findings suggest that A 60-something electrician has his very ordered life shattered by the sudden death of his wife. Left alone and forced to fend for himself in a strictly patriarchal society, he begins to recognize how much he took her devotion for granted. His attempts to reconnect with his estranged children are further complicated by his discovery that his son is living with another man.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Allan Deberton’s queer coming-of-age drama, which debuted in Berlin as part of the Generation Kplus section, follows a 12 year-old boy growing up in a small rural community trying balance his affection and desires with the fear of rejection from his father and surrounding community.

Check out a THR interview about the film here and the trailer below.

Nearly a decade after well-received 2017 feature Western, German director Valeska Grisebach returns with another deconstruction of a male-dominated genre. This slow-burning crime thriller, set in the Bulgarian borderlands, works as a low-key arthouse take on The Godfather, as archaeologist Veska (Yana Radeva) returns to the rural community she grew up in and reconnects with old friends, getting pulled back into criminal activity. Winner of the Jury Prize in Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Recent findings suggest that majid Majidi’s social drama, about Solan (Mohammad Rahimi), a poorly-paid temporary teacher in a remote, drought-stricken Iranian village was the stand out at this year’s Busan Film Festival, where it won the top prize, directly qualifying it for the Oscar race. When the death of the benefactor funding the school’s meal programme threatens to drive away the pupils, Solan takes matters into his own hands, turning to oil smuggling to keep the meals coming.

Check out the trailer for Midday Meal below.

Recent findings suggest that even the dead face eviction in Polen Ly’s elegiac ghost story about the cost of redevelopment in Cambodia. Thida (Savorn Serak) has watched over a movie house in Battambang since her death during the Khmer Rouge years. With the building marked for demolition, she must choose between wandering as a homeless spirit and risking the pain of another human life. She befriends Hai (Piseth Chhun), a young journalist who remembers going to the movies there as a boy. In the shuttered theater, the two watch a film together on his phone. Ly’s fiction feature debut premiered in Venice’s Biennale College Cinema program and won the Golden Hanoman, the top prize at Indonesia’s Jogja-NETPAC Asian Film Festival.

According to recent reports, nchini Sylvia-Bright is back in her second Cameroon Oscar submission after Ngang Romanus’ 2021 movie Hidden Dreams. In Mabanda, she plays Mojoko, a pregnant teenager who, after the death of her mother, is left alone with her abusive father, played by director Quintus, and faces rejection by her community. Shot in Cameroonian Pidgin English, it’s the eighth submission by the country for the Academy Awards.

Check out the first look trailer below.

Sources indicate that this transatlantic drama from Montreal-based director Geneviève Dulude-De Celles bowed in Berlin, where it won the Silver Bear for Best Screenplay. It centers on an art expert, Mihail, who fled Bulgaria 30 years earlier and returns to authenticate the work of Nina, an 8-year-old Bulgarian artist and possible child prodigy, whose paintings have gone viral online. As Mikhail studies her work, he is forced to confront the ghosts of his past.

Check out the trailer for Nina Rosa below.

The period mystery, the director’s second feature, premiered at Cannes. The follow-up to Martelli’s General Augusto Pinochet-era political thriller Chile ‘76is set in 1992, after Pinochet’s regime ends and a 9-year old girl is staying in an Andean ski resort where she befriends a German teenager aiming to be a competitive skier, only to vanish without a trace.

Read the THR review and an interview with Martelli.

Check out the trailer for The Meltdown below.

Chinese comedy star Shen Teng plays a chef who takes a job in Bahata, a fictional stand-in for Baghdad, to pay off his family’s debts. In this war drama loosely inspired by the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, the Chinese restaurant where he works becomes both a refuge for local orphans and a bar for American soldiers. Director Wen Muye previously made a blockbuster out of the high cost of cancer drugs in China with 2018’s Dying to Survive. This latest social drama has grossed $358.4 million worldwide, making it by far the highest-grossing entry in this year’s international feature Oscar race.

According to recent reports, A group of misfits converging at Babel, a legendary Colombian dive bar that doubles as purgatory, and where La Flaca — the city’s Grim Reaper — presides. Here, souls gamble years of their lives with her, daring to outwit Death herself. With his feature debut, which debuted at Sundance in 2025, director Gala del Sol has created a fantastical Colombian fever dream where life and death collides and the fate of people is left to chance.

Check out the official trailer below.

Sources indicate that with her debut feature, Costa Rica’s Kim Torres has created a rural chiller, combining story combining a coming-of-age drama with supernatural and thriller elements. The film follows 13-year-old Laura, who feels suffocated by her new family, despite the lush forests and palm plantations that surround her. She soon discovers the supposed village paradise hides a shadowy secret that preys on the women living in it. Torres’ drama world premiered at San Sebastian’s New Directors sidebar in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that director Hana Jusic took inspiration from Wuthering Heights and gothic horror in this period drama, set in rural Croatia, circa 1910, to tell a surprisingly modern tale of female liberation. Teresa, a Chilean woman dressed all in black like an avenging angel, arrives in an isolated, and deeply religious community of Croatian shepherds in the early 20th century, claiming to be the widow of a local man who emigrated to South America.

Sources indicate that her arrival unsettles the tightly ordered society, challenging its traditional relationships and expectations. Unable to speak the language, she becomes a blank canvas for hopes and fears, particularly of the women in the community.

You can read a director interview here and watch the THR Presents interview with Hana Jusic here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Industry observers note that carlos Larrazabal’s debut feature explores the pull of home and the longing to leave. It follows Elvis, who returns to Havana after spending a decade in prison for murdering his abusive stepfather. As he reconnects with childhood sweetheart and falls back into life in the city’s criminal underworld, Elvis must decide whether to stay in the world he knows or escape Havana for a new life elsewhere.

Cyprus’ first-ever international Oscar contender is also the feature debut of writer-director Myrsini Aristidou. Newcomer Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis, who played the son in Yorgos Lanthimos’ Dogtooth, star as an 11-year-old and her absent, petty criminal father who returns home after a family death. The film won The World Cinema Dramatic Audience Award at Sundance.

Check out the THR’s Presents interview with Myrsini Aristidou here and read an earlier interview with her here.

Prague-based filmmaker Pepa Lubojacki scoured through family photos and diary snapshots for this intimate, heart-rending look at her family’s struggles with alcoholism, addiction and homelessness. The film premiered in Berlin, where it won the best documentary honor as well as the independent Caligari award.

Recent findings suggest that this historical thriller from directors Yohane Dean Lengol and Hamed Mobasser is set in 1959, in the final months of Belgian colonial rule, in Club Rumba Royale, a popular nightclub where white Europeans and Congolese citizens rub shoulders as dance mixes with debates of independence. Featuring African rumba star Fally Ipupa, the feature is the first submission by DR Congo since 1997 and only the second overall.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

In a recent development, may el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion-winning Woman Unknown is backdropped by a Danish city free from Nazi occupation, mere months after World War II has ended. It tells the story of Marie (Volpi Cup winner Mathilde Arcel), a young nanny and housemaid about to marry her wealthy, older, and widowed employer, Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund). But Marie guards a shameful secret.

The Danish filmmaker deftly scrutinizes post-war patriotism and the era’s chastisement of women and their sex lives. “There have been so many films about the Second World War, and that is true,” el-Toukhy told THR ahead of Venice. “But they’re all based mostly on men’s experiences and recollections of war. So that really energized me.”.

Read THR‘s interview with May el-Toukhy here.

Check out a clip from Woman Unknown below.

According to recent reports, the second feature film from director Andrés Farías centers on Sonia (Mercedes Morales), a widow who trades her family home for a cramped apartment and finds unexpected intimacy with Aimé, a working-class Haitian man, defying her family and the racial tensions between Dominicans and Haitians. The drama played Havana, Miami and Chicago and won best film, director and actress at the 2026 Dominican Film Festival in New York.

Industry observers note that director Cristina Barragán, who represented Ecuador in 2016 with Alba, continues her exploration of childhood wounds in this drama starring Simone Bucio as Azucena, a woman in her 30s who approaches Julio, a teenager in a group home, played by first-time actor Francis Eddú Llumiquinga. As they spend time together, an uneasy closeness grows, changing the personal bond in ways two outsiders from different worlds, but with a shared experience of trauma, The film won the best screenplay award in the Orizzonti section at the Venice Film Festival.

Industry observers note that the Egyptian-Austrian filmmaker Abu Bakr Shawky is back in the international Oscar race after his 2018 feature Yomeddine, also submitted for Egypt. The Stories, loosely inspired by his own parents’ relationship, follows aspiring Cairo pianist Ahmed and his long-distance romance with Austrian pen pal Liz, from the 1960s through the 1980s. Starring Amir El-Masry (The Crown) and Valerie Pachner (Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore).

Read what the director mentioned about The Stories here and then check out the trailer below.

In a recent development, arturo López Rodas wrote, directed and produced this debut feature, a 60-minute drama in which three old friends reunite for a funeral after decades apart, musing on life, loss and time. It won best screenplay at the Ícaro Awards and best international feature at the Cobb International Film Festival. Vértices represents El Salvador’s first entry into Oscar’s best international feature competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

In his feature film debut, director German Golub charts the real-life story of Erika Salumäe, a track cyclist who overcomes personal and professional hardship — and the pressure of the dwindling Soviet regime — to become a two-time Olympic gold medallist in 1988 and 1992. From troubled young woman to national hero, Salumäe’s tenacity makes this biographical sports drama a story of inspiration and grit, with Estonian actress Karolin Jürise in the titular role.

Check out the trailer for Our Erika below.

It has been revealed that finnish filmmaker Markus Lehmusruusu (2019’s Ricky Rapper and the Strong Man) turns to science fiction in his sophomore feature. In a future, sterile world without nature or animals, Pasi (Miro Lopperi) is a lonely and compassionate designer of synthetic pets.

It has been revealed that when by chance he stumbles upon the last surviving squirrel, he decides to defy the very strict regulations of interaction with what little nature is left in the world and help the squirrel back into its natural habitat. Lehmusruusu tackles the intersection of humanity’s instinctive need to both survive and provide in this Fantastic Fest debut (which used real, trained squirrels over animatronics or VFX).

Check out the trailer for The Squirrel below.

Industry observers note that the first feature film from exiled Russian dissident director Andrey Zvyagintsev (Loveless, Leviathan) in nearly a decade is a taut psychological thriller set in Russia shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Loosely inspired by Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969) it follows a wealthy businessman caught between government demands that he recruit employees to send as cannon fodder in the war effort, and his growing suspicions that his wife is having an affair. As pressure mounts on both fronts, his carefully controlled domestic and professional life begins to unravel. Like the Russian state, he goes to extremes of violence to maintain the appearance of power and control.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Andrey Zvyagintsev here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Levan Koguashvili’s dramedy is set in a Georgian village struggling to recover from the economic upheaval following the collapse of the Soviet Union. At its center is Zuriko, a widowed hazelnut farmer trying to secure a fair price for his harvest while his debts mount. With the help of his friend Gela, he also embarks on a search for a new partner, despite the objections of his formidable former mother-in-law.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

In a recent development, birgit Minichmayr plays Ella, a mother struggling to process the death of her daughter Jessie, in Sandra Wollner’s drama about grief and the complicated bonds left behind. Ella begins spending time with Lux, Jessie’s boyfriend, who was with her on the night she died. As the two grow closer, their relationship becomes increasingly entangled with memories of the young woman. An impulsive family holiday to Tenerife becomes an increasingly surreal attempt to escape grief and reconnect with the past.

A favorite in Cannes, where it won Best Film of the Un Certain Regard section, Everytime has been nominated for Best Film and Wollner for Best Screenplay at the 2027 European Film Awards.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Sandra Wollner here.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

In a recent development, yannis Economides crafts a modern Greek tragedy out of the story of a businessman who devises what appears to be a foolproof scheme to save his family home from falling into the hands of a loan shark. But his plan sets a series of increasingly unpredictable events in motion, threatening to destroy the very life he is trying to preserve.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Guatemalan auteur Jayro Bustamante returns with an action-tinged drama inspired by the true story of Guatemala’s 2018 Volcán de Fuego tragedy. María Mercedes Coroy plays a volcanologist who tries to warn and evacuate Indigenous communities as a newly introduced volcano forms amid corruption and economic interests. This is Bustamante’s fourth Oscar submission, after 2015’s Ixcanul, 2019’s La Llorona (shortlisted) and Rita from 2024.

Check out the official trailer (no subtitles) below.

Snow falls on Hong Kong in Juno Mak’s underworld epic, in which a hospital bombing kills a pharmaceutical magnate and leaves his younger son with an unusual ambition for a family drug empire — to shut it all down. A long-in-the-making saga starring Asian industry heavyweights Takeshi Kaneshiro, Tony Leung Ka-fai and Louis Koo, the film premiered in Cannes and won eight Hong Kong Film Awards, including one for its score by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto.

It has been revealed that tony Leung Chiu-wai, Léa Seydoux and fast-rising German star Luna Wedler feature in this century-spanning contemplative drama from Hungarian auteur Ildikó Enyedi (On Body and Soul, The Story of My Wife). Set in three different eras — 1908, 1972, and 2020 — it follows three very different people, a pioneering female student, a lovesick young man and a Hong Kong neuroscientist who share a connection to an ancient ginkgo tree growing int the botanical garden of a German university town. Enigmatic but never self-serious, Silent Friend leavens its major ideas and visual poetry with a healthy dose of deadpan humor.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with Silent Friend star Luna Wedler here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

According to recent reports, yrsa Roca Fannberg turns her camera on the residents and caregivers of a Reykjavík nursing home in this observational documentary about ageing and the final stages of life. Everyday activities, from dancing and exercise classes to painting nails and sharing quiet moments, become the focus of an intimate portrait of a community negotiating the realities of old age. Rather than concentrating on decline, the film finds moments of companionship, humour and pleasure in the routines of institutional life.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Set in a remote Naga village near the Myanmar border in the early 1960s, Theja Rio’s debut feature follows Anghba, the community’s last surviving chief. With most of the villagers having left, he remains with his ailing wife and speech-impaired son, struggling to preserve the traditions of his ancestors. The arrival of an American missionary introduces Christianity and upcoming social customs, deepening the generational divide between father and son. The film won the Platform Award at Toronto, qualifying it for the Oscar race.

Read THR India‘s review of Angh here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In a recent development, in Santosh Davakhar’s Marathi-language folk thriller, a young bride in rural Maharashtra plots her groom’s murder during the traditional ceremony meant to bless their marriage. As the village gathers for the gondhal, an all-night ritual of devotional song and dance, Suman (Ishita Deshmukh) recruits the groom’s cousin, a former suitor, to do the killing so she can run away with one of the performers. The film won Davakhar the Silver Peacock for best director at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

Director Kamila Andini (Yuni) drew on the testimony of sexual assault survivors for this magical realist drama about the patriarchal structures of a Javanese mountain village. Putri Marino plays Pertiwi, who spent 20 years in prison for killing an accomplice to her rape at 16. She comes home to find the men who sent her away now running the village. When she meets a deaf teenage girl whose ordeal echoes her own, Pertiwi rallies her fellow outcasts to bring the abuse to light. The film premiered in Toronto, and Marino shared the best performance prize at the Singapore International Film Festival.

Babak Khajehpasha’s anti-war drama captures the lives and dreams of children and adults in Gaza against the backdrop of an ongoing conflict and crisis with Israel. The film cast child actors of Arab, Iranian, Syrian, and Lebanese backgrounds alongside Iranian performers.

Rather than depict violent battlefield scenes, the Iranian filmmaker focused on the all-too human impact of war on children as they learn fear, death and waiting are part of their everyday lives. The film also strikes a note of hope that love and life can be kept alive during horrific war and strife.

The Iraqi feature, which premiered out of competition in Venice, follows a female Kurdish sniper, Vyan, who returns to Mosul to try and rescue her younger sister. She has survived war by suppressing her emotions. When she learns that her younger sister, missing since the ISIS assault in 2014, may still be alive, she goes all out to rescue her. Mustafa, who was born in Iraqi Kurdistan and fled to Norway as a child, found inspiration for the film from an encounter with a female Peshmerga sniper during the 2014 frontline battles, as female Kurdish fighters countered Islamic State attacks.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Industry observers note that A robbery at a rural credit union ends in tragedy, but Damian McCann’s Irish-language thriller works backwards to reveal how three women became involved in the botched operation. Carrie Crowley, Bríd Brennan and Eva-Jane Gaffney star as the unlikely accomplices at the center of a story involving desperation, criminal ambition and a woman on the verge of a breakdown.

Check out the trailer for Aontas below.

The Israeli film, set in 1987, centers on a 12-year-old boy, Boaz, who while preparing for his bar mitzvah is shocked to witness his father having sex in a swimming pool locker room. The boy’s family life is upturned just as the AIDS epidemic takes hold. But a decade later, the father and his older son attempt to reconcile and accept one another.

Rosenthal’s film, titled Independence in Hebrew, premiered at Sundance and won the top best picture award at Israel’s Ophir Awards, automatically making it the country’s Academy Awards entry.

Check out the trailer for Tell Me Everything below.

It has been revealed that paolo Strippoli’s psychological thriller is one of the rare genre romps among the mostly serious dramas in this season’s international Oscar race. Jasmine Trinca plays a housewife so desperate to have the perfect family she makes a faustian bargain with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi’s chain-smoking stranger, triggering a series of events that, over the course of decades, will bring her family crashing down. Fresh Line has already snatched up English remake rights to this twisty crowd pleaser.

Read THR‘s review of The Spiral here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s first French feature begins as a workplace drama set in a nursing home outside Paris and blossoms into a love story about two women falling for each other’s minds. Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira) asks her overstretched nurses to employ a more humane system of care for residents living with dementia. Watching a play about life in a psychiatric institution, she recognizes her own convictions in the work of its Japanese director, Mari (Tao Okamoto), who is dying of cancer.

Industry observers note that the women connect and talk deep into the night, slipping between French and Japanese, and there’s such pleasure in their exchanges that even Mari’s impromptu whiteboard lecture on capitalism feels like a moment of deep emotional connection. Efira and Okamoto shared the best actress prize at Cannes. After winning the international feature Oscar for Drive My Car in 2022, Hamaguchi is again considered a frontrunner this season.

Read THR‘s interview with All of a Sudden co-stars Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira here.

The film’s official trailer is below.

It has been revealed that sink is a drama about a mother navigating her son’s mental health crisis — still a taboo subject in Jordan — by denying her son’s struggles and opting instead to see his emotional withdrawal and disruptive behavior at school as teenage rebellion. So the mother follows her son about with devotion, hoping her guidance at attention will prove a cure. Duraie’s debut feature, following her acclaimed short films Horizon and Give up the Ghost, had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival, nd.

Abel is a shepherd living on a collective farm in Kazakhstan whose life in thrown into turmoil in the 1990s when, following the collapse of the Soviet Union, collective farms were dismantled and divided up among corrupt leaders. The aging Abel has a choice: play along for a piece of the action or stand up for what he believes is right.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

In a recent development, writer-director Vincho Nchogu serves up a mix of comedy and drama in her feature debut. Sarah Karei plays Star, an orphaned and unmarried 38-year-old woman in a rural village who risks losing her home unless she can prove her family lineage and claim her land deed. Along the way she has to deal with hostile neighbors, shady organizations and the promise of potential romance. Winner of the audience award at Tribeca and the Best First Feature prize at the BFI London Film Festival.

According to recent reports, blerta Basholli takes a coming-of-age story into the increasingly volatile atmosphere of late-1990s Kosovo. Thirteen-year-old Dua is navigating the usual uncertainties of adolescence when an incident turns her into a target within her community. Her friendship with the outspoken Maki offers a new perspective on the world around her, even as the escalating conflict threatens to overwhelm their lives.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

It has been revealed that bekzat Pirmatov blends psychological horror, folklore and family drama in this supernatural tale about a grieving woman plagued by a recurring nightmare in which an unseen presence appears to strangle her in her sleep. Seeking an explanation, she turns to a traditional healer who discovers ominous markings on the bodies of pregnant women. Their investigation leads to the ancient Kyrgyz legend of Albarsty, a malevolent female spirit associated with pregnancy and childbirth.

A biographical sports drama from Viesturs Kairišs, who co-wrote Ulya with Kārlis Arnolds Avots, Livia Ulman, and Andris Feldmanis. The Cannes-premiering, black-and-white feature is set in rural Soviet Latvia in 1964, where Uļjana “Ulya” Semjonova’s (Kārlis Arnolds Avots) attracts the attention of basketball scouts due to her exceptional height and strength. She’s pulled from farm life into elite sport in this mise-en-scène-embracing portrait of a Latvian legend.

Read THR‘s interview with director Viesturs Kairišs here.

Check out THR‘s portrait of Ulya star and co-screenwriter Karlis Arnolds Avots here.

Sources indicate that lebanon’s Oscar hopeful is a heist thriller about two sisters who concoct an elaborate blueprint to break into a bank to steal their own money — the cash frozen by the government during the 2019 Lebanese liquidity crisis — to fund a life-saving operation. Director Rami Kodeih co-wrote the film with his wife Nora Mariana inspired by their own experience at the time, when Mariana needed surgery and their savings were inaccessible. George Clooney and Grant Heslov are executive producers for Smokehouse Pictures.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out a clip from the film below.

How to Divorce During the War is exactly as it sounds — a high-flying executive Marija (Zygimante Elena Jakstaite) chooses the worst possible moment to inform her struggling filmmaker husband Vytas (Marius Repsys) she wants to split up: just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Vilnius-set, soul-searching drama won director Andrius Blaževičius a directing award upon its Sundance premiere.

In a recent development, this jump scare-heavy psychological horror from debut feature filmmaker Cyrus Neshvad (already an Oscar nominee for 2023 short The Red Suitcase) follows a family in dire straits. With their young son not having much time left, Anne and Greg are ready to sacrifice everything to give him one last chance at salvation. But after crossing an unforgivable moral line, they find themselves trapped in a nightmare where every choice comes with an ever-higher price. Child earned its world premiere at the 2026 Raindance Film Festival.

Check out the official trailer below.

Recent findings suggest that woo Ming Jin drew on his own childhood as a twin for this coming-of-age drama about two teenage brothers in a Malaysian coastal town. At 15, Ali is the only person who understands his twin brother Amir’s way of communicating. When their father remarries, he packs the boys off to work in a salted-fish factory. But it’s their shared crush on their upcoming English teacher (Indonesian star Dian Sastrowardoyo) that turns the brothers into rivals. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival.

Industry observers note that żejtune is a visually rich Maltese-language drama from the Latest York-based Alex Camilleri, led by Michela Farrugia as Mar. When her estranged mother passes away, Mar sees her way out of Malta by selling off her inheritance: three pieces of farmland in the countryside. On her journey to claim her land, she meets Nenu, a spirited 80-year-old singer (Nenu Borg) whose vibrant folk music pulls her into the colourful traditions of the island she’s been so eager to escape. The movie hit the festival circuit with appearances at Gothenburg and Tribeca.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

David Pablos’ drama follows Veneno (Víctor Prieto), a rebellious young drifter who sleeps with truckers at roadside diners. He persuades one of his hook ups, Muñeco (Osvaldo Sánchez) to take him deep into the hyper-masculine world of long-haul trucking. The road movie, produced by Diego Luna, won best film in Venice’s Orizzonti section as well as the Queer Lion.

Read THR‘s review of On The Road here.

Sources indicate that mongolia’s struggle to end more than two centuries of Qing rule takes the shape of an espionage thriller in Tamir Bat-Ulzii’s sweeping historical epic. The actor-director casts himself as Namnansuren, the statesman who joined forces with the Buddhist leader Bogd Khan in 1911. The conspirators seek help from Russia while building a network of spies at home. Made to mark the 115th anniversary of Mongolia’s declaration of independence, the film became one of the country’s biggest local hits this year.

Industry observers note that biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić drummed up excitement in Sundance with To Hold a Mountain, a documentary shot in the Montenegrin highlands where a shepherdess and her adopted daughter are haunted by the violent death of her mother and must defend their mountain against its transformation into a NATO military training ground. This tender, windswept feature picked up the Grand Jury Prize in Sundance and the Heart of Sarajevo in the fest’s documentary competition section.

It has been revealed that laïla Marrakchi offers a new spin on the familiarly-bleak tale of migrant labor and exploitation in this social realist drama, inspired by real-life cases of Moroccan women who travel to Spain to work as seasonal fruit-pickers. Her protagonist Hasna (Nisrin Erradi) is a flawed, even unlikable character doing what she needs to survive in a world where oppression and coercion are the norm. Strawberries premiered in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section.

Read THR‘s interview with Laila Marrakchi here.

Abinash Bikram Shah’s debut, the first Nepali feature to screen in Cannes’ Official Selection, won the jury prize in Un Certain Regard. The richly-realized missing-person thriller follows Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama), the matriarch of a Kinnar community of trans women in rural Nepal. Pirati dreams of slipping away with the man she loves. But when one of the young women she calls her daughters vanishes on a night patrol to keep wild elephants out of the village, she puts those aims on hold to search for her.

Read THR India’s interview with Abinash Bikram Shah here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Sources indicate that afghan-Dutch filmmaker Dawood Hilmandi turns the camera on his own family history in this intimate documentary about war, exile and an attempt at reconciliation with his estranged father. Having fled Afghanistan and later Iran, Hilmandi has made a home in Amsterdam, but a personal loss prompts him to return to his father, an aging, authoritarian former mujahideen fighter. Together they revisit the past, travelling between Iran and Afghanistan in an effort to overcome decades of silence, inherited trauma and estrangement. The film won three prizes at IDFA, including Best First Feature and the FIPRESCI international critics award.

Check out the trailer for Paikar below.

Industry observers note that sisters Ade and Titi lead very different lives under the shadow of their late father. The older Ade (Bimbo Akintola) is a devout Christian and the family’s sole breadwinner, while Titi (Tosin Adeyemi) is an aspiring singer full of independent spirit. When their ailing mother comes to live with them, old resentments resurface, forcing both sisters to confront grief and the fragile bonds that hold a family together.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Kosara Mitić’s debut feature 17, co-written by Ognjen Sviličić, arrived at this year’s Berlinale with a fierce exploration of sexual trauma and female solidarity. The movie follows seventeen-year-old Sara (Eva Kostic), who’s hiding a secret during a school trip. When the trip spirals out of control and she witnesses her friend Lina being sexually assaulted, the two girls try to break the cycle of casual violence and seal an everlasting bond between them in the process.

Read THR‘s interview with 17 director Kosara Mitić here.

Hans Petter Moland adapts Knut Hamsun’s Nobel Prize-winning novel about a man determined to make a life in the Norwegian wilderness. Isak arrives in the remote landscape with little more than his willingness to work the land. His relationship with Inger leads to a family and a more permanent settlement, but the couple’s struggle to survive the harsh conditions is gradually complicated by the arrival of the outside world.

Check out the trailer for The Growth of the Soil below.

In August 2023, eight passengers, six of them schoolboys, found themselves dangling in a cable car 900 feet above a ravine in northern Pakistan. Mohammed Ali Naqvi pieced together what followed from cellphone and drone footage, interviews and re-creations, as army commandos and local volunteers raced to save them. The film premiered at Sundance and is the first documentary Pakistan has submitted for the international feature Oscar.

Read THR’s review of Hanging by a Wire here.

Read THR‘s interview with Mohammed Ali Naqvi here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Industry observers note that osama is a professional photographer, and fresh father, living in Gaza who, at the start of the Gaza war, turns to photojournalism to support his wife and infant child. This period drama is freely inspired by the 1959 killing of radio host Bernardo Aranda, which led the Paraguay dictatorship to persecute gay men. #128747. DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions?
  • Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA.
  • Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.

Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

The research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides latest insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.

Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists.

One of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An important difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.

This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.

Industry observers note that why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.

To explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.

DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage.

Sources indicate that the results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an key advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.

"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," stated Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule.".

This finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.

The discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an important role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.

Newly introduced Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection.

Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.

The team established a upcoming set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.

"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," remarked Khosh Abady.

These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.

Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?

With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team strategy to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.

Industry observers note that A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.

It has been revealed that "We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," mentioned Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins.".

By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nitesh Tiwari’s “Ramayana” has doubled visitor numbers at Kerala’s Jatayu Earth’s Center, known locally as Jatayu Rock, Ministry of Tourism joint secretary Harikishore S.
  • It has been revealed that producers on the same stage noted crew skill and speed give India an edge, though Sunita Ram of Rasika Pictures warned the country still lacks the studio space to keep its biggest shoots at home.
  • The session, “Filming in India: India’s Rise as a Global Production Hub,” featured Prithul Kumar, joint secretary, broadcasting, at the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting; Harikishore; Alan McAlex, founder of Suitable Pictures (“Santosh,” “Sister Midnight”); and Ram, whose Rasika Pictures handles service production and co-productions (“A Suitable Boy,” “120 Bahadur”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nitesh Tiwari’s “Ramayana” has doubled visitor numbers at Kerala’s Jatayu Earth’s Center, known locally as Jatayu Rock, Ministry of Tourism joint secretary Harikishore S. told a WAVES Film Bazaar panel in Goa, where Indian officials pitched a single-window filming portal and state incentives to international producers. The site is traditionally held to be where the mythical bird Jatayu fell after battling Ravana, a fight the film depicts.

It has been revealed that producers on the same stage noted crew skill and speed give India an edge, though Sunita Ram of Rasika Pictures warned the country still lacks the studio space to keep its biggest shoots at home. Related Stories Mike Newell Recalls Being Shot at in Colombia While Filming ‘Love in the Time of Cholera’ With Giovanna Mezzogiorno: ‘She Was Like, “F— All This!”’.

The session, “Filming in India: India’s Rise as a Global Production Hub,” featured Prithul Kumar, joint secretary, broadcasting, at the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting; Harikishore; Alan McAlex, founder of Suitable Pictures (“Santosh,” “Sister Midnight”); and Ram, whose Rasika Pictures handles service production and co-productions (“A Suitable Boy,” “120 Bahadur”).

Kumar remarked the India Cine Hub portal first went live at Film Bazaar on Nov. 21, 2015. At the time, it mainly handled film visas and permissions for foreign productions. In 2023, the ministry widened its scope after concluding that overseas producers also needed support on the ground and a way to find local resources. The portal now combines permission applications with directories of crew, equipment and services, an interactive location map, and information on state and central incentives.

In a recent development, state governments, local administrations and central agencies including the Railways, the Archaeological Survey of India and the civil aviation authorities, which clear drone use, all sit behind the single window. Each state has a nodal officer who follows up on permissions in person, Kumar said.

“It’s a hundred times more difficult than manufacturing or assembling a product because every step is a latest one, and the filmmakers actually have to turn dreams into reality,” Kumar said of filmmaking.

It has been revealed that he clarified that the portal is a permissions tool rather than a networking one; collaboration between filmmakers and service providers happens on the separate WAVES Bazaar market platform. Kumar also said the Ministry of Tourism has signed a non-binding, non-commercial MoU with production houses including Netflix, Amazon and JioCinema to encourage more content about India, such as its food, rivers and forests, and to encourage them to shoot in a wider range of places.

Kumar also asked filmmakers in the room to list themselves on India Cine Hub so producers anywhere in the world can find them.

In a recent development, harikishore said roughly 80% of what a producer needs comes from the states, with the central ministry handling the other 20%. He pointed to Madhya Pradesh, which he said pays back up to 75% of the cost of a film shot in the state. “And it is not a policy paper; they have given it to 50 people in the last two years,” Harikishore said.

He remarked the jump in visitors at the site is set to last. In his view, what holds other locations back is a knowledge gap among state decision-makers about what productions actually want, and he proposed workshops in which producers brief officials. Kumar agreed, noting that states tend to upload only tourist landscapes to the portal. “Shooting happens in a village, it happens in a house,” Kumar said. The ministry has also asked states to pick 10 locations from past hit films and brand them, he added, citing Bekal Fort, where a song from “Bombay” was shot. Kumar said Jatayu Rock should likewise carry “Ramayana” branding.

McAlex stated India used to draw productions mainly when scripts had Indian stories or characters. “We had projects coming in to shoot American interiors because the actors had a very short window, so they didn’t have to go back to the U.S.,” McAlex said. He added that AI and volume stages are now opening the door to exterior work too, and that local crews and VFX facilities let productions keep everything in one place.

According to recent reports, as examples of Indian crews pulling off complex work, he cited a British Film Institute-funded project whose executives doubted a mid-day company move in Mumbai could be done. His team managed it. He also pointed to an American production on which only the director and DP flew in, and an all-Indian crew pulled off a stunt sequence on a fifth floor.

Ram mentioned international producers are now confident that Indian working standards match those of the U.K., Europe and the U.S., and that they no longer need to fly in large teams when they can mix in local crew. “Every day of shoot is like, you know, launching a rocket every day. But that’s world over, not just India,” Ram said. She tells anyone who doubts what’s possible in India that 24 hours there can equal three weeks of work elsewhere, because “we can turn things around here faster than anywhere else.”.

Ram added that she looks for upcoming locations with every script. One recent project set in Mumbai ended up shooting in the small town of Karaikudi instead. “They’d never even heard of it, but it’s something you introduce, you know, with every film,” she said.

WAVES Film Bazaar is the market component of the International Film Festival of India.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.
  • It has been revealed that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.

It has been revealed that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S. has shifted in recent years. In 2010, about 60% of clothing was predominantly made from cotton. Now, that total is around 45%, while predominantly synthetic fabrics such as polyester and nylon comprise the majority of imports.

According to recent reports, apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. Since 2020, they have soared to record highs.

It has been revealed that it's starting to change habits for consumers who are paying more for food, gas, rent and other staples. As shoppers shell out more for clothes, they're increasingly making sure the garments are worth the cost.

Consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index, which surveyed more than 9,000 shoppers, found that consumers are scrutinizing labels more closely and rejecting cheap materials sold at a premium.

"If it's not a natural material, a retailer brand who passes it off as it is, they're really becoming very low on consumers' minds," mentioned Sonia Lapinsky, head of fashion at AlixPartners.

Sources indicate that fast fashion brands like Forever 21 and H&M exploded in popularity during the early 2000s and 2010s, bringing trendy clothing to shelves swiftly at low prices. Then came ultra-fast fashion, with brands like Shein and Fashion Nova pumping out new garments at even quicker speeds and lower price points — made possible in part through the use of inexpensive, synthetic fabrics.

Recent findings suggest that "We got to a point where the pendulum just swung too far in that direction. And we've actually begun to see a reversal," said U.S. Bancorp BTIG consumer analyst Janine Stichter. "Quality matters a lot more ... over the last three or four years than it has in the previous 10 or 20.".

But quality, which shoppers often tie directly to material, can come at a higher cost.

Recent findings suggest that the average unit price of apparel imported to the U.S. between January and August was $2.64 per square meter for garments that were predominantly synthetic fiber, like polyester and nylon, compared with $3.67 for items that were largely cotton, according to data from the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Textiles and Apparel.

When comparing those 2026 figures to 2010, synthetic fiber apparel import costs have climbed around 11%, while cotton apparel costs have risen 21%.

"If you're appealing to a more value-sensitive customer, you either reduce the quality, or you negotiate with suppliers to try to share some of the cost or you maybe absorb the cost … and perhaps hope to crank a higher volume of product to make up for it," remarked Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman.

Though polyester is cheaper, experts point out that's not necessarily a bad thing. It can help clothing hold its shape and wick away sweat.

Recent findings suggest that sherman believes the athleisure boom is a primary factor in the shift toward polyester. She noted that from 2015 to 2025, sports apparel was growing at a 4.9% rate in the U.S., versus 2.6% for all apparel and footwear, according to Euromonitor data.

"There probably is some quality trade down as well happening there," Sherman said. "But I think both these trends are conflated.".

Industry observers note that nonetheless, backlash to synthetic materials is growing. Gen Z has even repurposed the word "polyester" as an insult to mean generally low-quality or fake.

Concerns have also grown about the environment and human health surrounding petroleum-based clothing, as more research indicates microplastics can leach from polyester clothing when washed.

It's led consumers to reexamine what materials are in their clothing.

According to recent reports, apparel prices have risen coming out of the pandemic, as demand outpaced supply and allowed companies to raise prices, mentioned BTIG's Stichter. Tariffs and the Iran war followed, raising costs for businesses — and prices for consumers.

Petroleum is the basis of many synthetic fibers, and oil prices have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.

The same factors that helped drive up prices of clothing — Covid, tariffs and war — also affected clothing quality.

"Companies had to move around their supply chains in the post-Covid period," said Stichter. "They had to find ways to take costs out, and sometimes that meant using less expensive fabrics.".

Those factors compounded a more-than-decade-long shift away from manufacturing in China.

Sheng Lu, a fashion and apparel studies professor at the University of Delaware, whose research focuses on the economics of the global textile industry, said China's established history with clothing production means it has higher-skilled workers, state-of-the-art-equipment and better material management compared with emerging manufacturing destinations such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.

It has been revealed that "They mostly serve the value market and the mass market. And I think the reason why they're not ready to make higher-quality luxury and premium products really reflects the kind of skill sets you can expect when you source from these countries," said Lu.

AlixPartners' Lapinsky said these countries that manufacture at a lower cost sometimes have to still ship the raw materials from China, which can extend the timeline to make clothing. That means taking earlier bets on trends and then discounting if products don't sell well.

"If you have to mark down that product because the consumer doesn't want it as much, your net margin might actually be worse than if you were to just invest in quality in the first place," mentioned BTIG's Stichter.

And as material costs rise for synthetic fibers, Stichter also said she believes it could further influence companies to use more natural fabrics moving forward.

Companies prioritizing quality are winning in this environment.

Ralph Lauren's stock is up around 85% over the past two years. Around 90% of its apparel is primarily made of cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. In its fiscal 2026, the tech giant remarked it sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns.

Meanwhile, direct-to-consumer clothing brand Quince, which centers its brand identity around natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation this year.

The brand jumped 16 spots to No. 3 for best resale value in online consignment retailer ThredUp's 2025 report. Organic cotton retailer Pact jumped 20 spots on that list to No. 8, illustrating the potential role materials are playing in brand recognition.

Industry observers note that alternatively, the 2026 AlixPartners report, which ranks sentiment for brands in different retail categories, found shoppers are viewing some fast fashion brands less favorably. Both Shein and Zara dropped three spots — to fifth and seventh place, respectively — in terms of sentiment in the young adult specialty category.

Industry observers note that shein passed higher tariff costs onto shoppers in 2025 and then blamed a sales slowdown on those higher prices. The ultra-fast fashion retailer saw its year-over-year share of U.S. apparel, accessories and footwear card spending decrease in the fourth quarter of 2025 and first two quarters of 2026, according to Consumer Edge.

Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sources indicate that though Zara fell in AlixPartners' Consumer Sentiment Index, it has continued to grow sales and profits year over year. Even so, Lapinsky said worsening consumer views are something to watch, even if the firm is doing well.

"What we found over the years with this consumer sentiment index is that sometimes it will be a bit of a leading indicator of what's to come," noted AlixPartners' Lapinsky. "I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara, but I think that's one thing that we'll be watching as we look in the upcoming quarters and into 2027.".
